speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to inform hon. members that the Canadian Wheat Board, following negotiations in Canton, has succeeded in concluding a sales contract with the People's Republic of China to provide for the export of 1.5 million long tons, 5 per cent more or less, of wheat to be shipped between December 1968 and July 1969 principally from Pacific coast ports.
This contract is under the provisions of the third long term agreement with China and consists of No. 4 northern and No. 5 wheat and limited quantities of Garnet and winter wheat.
Assuming that full tolerance is taken, the sale amounts to 58.5 million bushels.
Including the contract covered by this announcement, total sales under the third long term agreement amount to 6.3 million tons or approximately 235 million bushels. The long term agreement provides for a minimum of 168 million bushels and a maximum of 280 million bushels over the three year period commencing August 1, 1966, with the amounts for each year to be negotiated separately.
As in the previous contracts, payment terms for sales under the long term agreement are 25 per cent cash when each vessel is loaded, and the balance of 75 per cent in 18 months with interest. The deferred payment provision is made possible by a guarantee to the Canadian Wheat Board by the government of Canada.

I extend to the Canadian Wheat Board my sincere congratulations on this successful sales effort.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO DISCONTINUE ADDITIONAL PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Latin you have just read, fructus aequitur labori, indicates the essence of the bill. That phrase means "Let the remuneration equal the work." Our parliamentary secretaries have had some of their functions restricted by the Prime Minister's announcement that we are to have a system of ministers, acting ministers and second acting ministers. As a consequence the position of parliamentary secretary becomes more honorary than actual. The position of committee chairman is far more exacting. I therefore submit that we now ought to remove from the Parliamentary Secretaries Act the provision that there shall be paid an additional $4,000 per annum to parliamentary secretaries.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Chairman, as I said, the intent of this measure is to enable leaders of the opposition parties to avail themselves of some technical facilities, to resort to the services of economists, sociologists, jurists, and to alleviate their difficult duty in criticizing the government's legislative measures. As everyone knows, these pieces of legislation are usually excellent, so that the task of criticizing them is even more difficult. It,is time that we realize the necessity of taking the utmost advantage of the time available to us.
For many decades, we have been realizing that the business of the house is ever increasing. The number of session days has had to be increased with the years, but we have now reached the limit of this possibility. It is

necessary to be more efficient in the use of these days, and it is obvious that, in our parliamentary system, the opposition has an important part to play and that it is in the national interest to make public funds available to them in order that they may discharge their duty with full knowledge of the facts.

For these reasons we have examined a number of different methods of assisting the leaders of the opposition parties. We examined, for example, a suggestion submitted by an hon. member of an opposition party that a sum of money be allocated to each caucus based on the number of members of that caucus. This is an interesting idea. It would, of course, be very helpful to the government party because our caucus comprises a great number of members. However, we felt that the first step in the expenditure of public funds was not to assist the caucus members but to assist the leaders. As hon. members know, research facilities are already provided to the backbenchers by the parliamentary library staff. These facilities have been used frequently by a certain number of members. I feel that if the time comes when more demand is put on these research staffs we may have to consider increasing their size, but for the time being the system is working well. Backbenchers in all parties may call upon the members of the parliamentary library staff for assistance in their research and even to do some writing for them.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
The intent in this particular item is to help the leaders of the parties in view of the fact that the opposition parties have a distinct role to play under our parliamentary system. We have decided to do this by allotting a substantial amount of money to the Leader of the Opposition and a lesser amount to the leaders of the other parties which are recognized under the rules and regulations of the house, that is, those parties which have more than 12 members.
The intention is, of course, not that these funds be employed for political organization or narrow partisan purposes but that they be employed directly as an aid to parliamentary work. For this reason, an agreement has been reached between myself and the Leader of the Opposition, as well as the leaders of the other parties, whereby funds would be allocated to them. Under this item research personnel will be hired by the Speaker of the house or by the clerk on the recommendation

of the leaders of these parties. It is intended that certain positions will be established. In this way there will be some minimum basis on which this house can discuss these estimates when they come up in succeeding years, and ensure that the funds are employed for this particular, agreed purpose.
I should go on to say that I have had very helpful co-operation from the Leader of the Opposition and from the leaders of the other parties. We have arrived at this plan without too much discussion. This step can be viewed as a first step in assisting the opposition parties and members of parliament generally to discharge their duties. This step, we felt, was the most urgent one and since it entails the expenditure of public funds we wanted to begin with this step before considering other methods.
I have one final word, Mr. Chairman, and that is to thank the Leader of the Opposition and the leaders of other parties for their cooperation in this matter. I should like to express the hope that the result will be, not more informed debate because the opposition debaters are always informed, but that the information will come to the fore sooner in the debate so that they will be in a position to perhaps shorten the length of time which is spent on one bill.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to express my appreciation to the right hon. Prime Minister for what I think we all must regard happily as a very constructive measure taken by the Prime Minister and his government to assist the opposition parties in their role which is, from year to year, growing more and more complex. I express the hope that as the opposition becomes more informed it will not follow what is sometimes the tendency of those who become full of learning, that is, to speak at even greater length. I hope this will not be the result; indeed, I am sure it will not be. It is clear, I think, that the scope of government operations is becoming broader and broader from year to year as governments, one way and another, seem to become more and more involved in more and more of the affairs of the citizen and of the community. It is clear that if the opposition parties are to meet the government in this house on anything approaching equal terms so far as information is concerned, facilities must be provided in addition to those that prevail today. The government has at its disposal, of course, an excellent public service and can also consult

those who are well informed outside the ranks of the public service.
The Prime Minister referred to the excellence of the legislation and therefore the need of the opposition perhaps becoming even more urgent. He will forgive me if I say to him that in view of the various positions of the government this session I have not so far felt the need of any additional assistance of this sort, but I am sure that time will come and the assistance therefore is timely. It is obviously impossible for members of the opposition parties to be well informed on all the matters that come before the house. I would say also that it would be impossible for our caucus, for example, to be well informed simply with the assistance of the staff that we will now be able to provide. Although the provision is generous, nevertheless the staff will be small and the caucus will be unable to make itself well informed on all matters on which the government is involved, such as estimates and the various other matters the government is likely to bring before the house.
This staff must serve the leader, the caucus and the members of the caucus in their work. While members of the caucus can get assistance from the parliamentary library on matters that concern them individually, the members and the caucus are also concerned with caucus positions on matters that come before the house. This staff, therefore, in this sense must serve the caucus and serve the members of the caucus.
I say this now so there will be no possibility of misunderstanding. The Prime Minister referred to this fund and the staff being used directly in the legislative work. He, I am sure, will be among the first to recognize that if I and my caucus are to be well informed in depth on various matters about which the government is concerned we will also have to utilize well informed people outside of the house and outside of this staff because this will be a relatively small staff to be informed in depth on all matters. There will of necessity, therefore, need to be some liaison between this staff and perhaps an advisory committee outside the confines of parliament so that the staff cap draw upon the informed opinions of those outside the house. I trust that this would not be regarded as a type of partisan liaison beyond the scope of the arrangement described by the Prime Minister.
The task of such a group is obviously a complex one which obviously requires a competent structure of organization. The
November 15, 1968

success of this staff will, of course, depend in particular upon the calibre of the head of the research team. As I have indicated, he will have to serve not only myself but also the caucus collectively and the caucus individually along the lines I have indicated. We will proceed as rapidly as we can but our aim, of course, will be to provide a staff high in quality, and this may take a little time.
I rise, Mr. Chairman, in particular to express my personal thanks and the thanks of this party for the constructive measures that the Prime Minister has taken in this regard.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, Hansard will indicate that we are discussing an item having to do with the residence of the Speaker of the Senate, but as we are all now aware we are in fact discussing a supplementary item that was tabled this morning by the President of the Treasury Board which provides an extra sum of money for the general administration of the House of Commons, in particular that section of the administration that comes under the authority of the Clerk.
I regret very much that other commitments and responsibilities have made it impossible for the parliamentary leader of this group, the hon. member for York South, to be here on this occasion, and I know that he too will regret very much that he was not able to be here for this discussion. It puts me, Mr. Chairman, in the position of not only having to speak for him but of trying to say the things that he would want said at this time.
I think the first thing that I have to say on his behalf, Mr. Chairman, is that he welcomes the attention that the Prime Minister has given to his request that something be done in this area. Naturally he and all of us in this party welcome any first step that is being taken. However, I think I would have to say that the agreement that the Prime Minister said was arrived at between him and the parliamentary leader of this party was not, at least so far as the hon. member for York South was concerned of the happiest kind.
I believe that while the negotiations were being carried on he continued to urge upon the Prime Minister, the President of the Privy Council and others that there be certain modifications in the proposal that is now before us. Perhaps there will be an opportunity for the hon. member for York South to speak for himself on this particular aspect, but I felt that I should on his behalf enter
Supply-Legislature
this caveat. I see the Prime Minister is nodding his head. In other words, I am saying yes, there was an agreement, but the hon. member for York South agreed only because the Prime Minister would not go any farther.
At any rate, Mr. Chairman, I think that the house in general should take this opportunity to express its approval of the action of the government in calling upon parliament to devote a certain portion of public funds to this kind of purpose. After all, it does not make sense to elect 264 people to the job that is ours in parliament, to pay us $12,000 a year to do the job, and then to be skimpy when it comes to providing the kind of assistance and service that we need in order to do our job effectively. Maybe some of us have got along for a good many years without this kind of assistance, but the job is getting that much more complicated and we do think it could be done better if research and other kinds of assistance were made available not just to the leaders of the various parties but to members of the house generally.
The Prime Minister said that one of the opposition party leaders had suggested a different approach. It is no secret that that suggestion was made by the hon. member for York South. It was that this kind of assistance should be provided not just to party leaders but to all members of parliament as such. The way we operate in this house, Mr. Chairman, this means the members of the various parties in the House of Commons.
The Prime Minister will recall that when the hon. member for York South first made his proposal to the Prime Minister-indeed, Mr. Chairman, I was with the hon. member at the time-the suggestion was made that this kind of assistance should be made available to members of all parties, including those on the government side of the house. I recognize the validity of the Prime Minister's statement that there are a lot of members over there; in fact, there is no doubt that there are too many. But if this kind of assistance is not made available to them, it does leave the notion that somehow they have access to the public service, to government sources, that is not available to those on this side of the house. That is not really true. I find that the public service generally is just as responsive to my requests for information as it could possibly be to the request of anybody else. However, if I were a backbench Liberal I think I would be complaining bitterly about a proposal that provides extra assistance to

November 15, 1968
Supply-Legislature
members of opposition parties but no assistance as such to members on the government side of the house.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: hope that the "hear, hears" and the loud applause at this point, particularly from the backbenchers on the government side, is recorded in Hansard.
I am willing to say that that is a good idea, but it does cost more money.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Then that is fine; the response is almost unanimous, Mr. Chairman.
We are now spending a lot of money on the running of the House of Commons, some $15 million. That does not include the $3 million to run the Senate of which I do not approve. But if we are spending that much money and electing presumably capable, efficient and skilled people to do the biggest piece of work that has to be done in this country, namely, the job of running the country itself, then I do not think it is unreasonable or irresponsible to spend whatever few more dollars are necessary to enable such people to keep up with the kind of tasks that have to be tackled here in parliament. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, while expressing to the government the formal thanks of the hon. member for York South and of this group for taking this step, may I say that if my deskmate were here he would be speaking pretty strongly about this matter, insisting that this is really only a gesture and that the government ought to be going a great deal farther.
Perhaps the Prime Minister's defence will be that this is a beginning, but I did not like the way in which he placed so much emphasis on the provision being of assistance just to the leaders of the other parties. The Leader of the Opposition stated the obvious, namely, that the assistants that he will employ will not be just for his use but for the group as a whole. I know that we in our party have the same intention. Our leader has no thought of just using whatever money is made available to him to increase the staff in the leader's office. He is determined that any money that is made available will be used to hire research people to assist the members of this party as a whole. So why not put it on that basis, Mr. Chairman, and provide this assistance for all our members, for all the Conservatives, for all the Creditistes and for all the Liberals?

The Prime Minister made reference to the research division of the Parliamentary Library and to the assistance that we are able to get there. I join with him and others in paying tribute to the assistance we have received from that division. However, Mr. Chairman, I point out that cabinet ministers do not rely just on impartial, objective people like librarians to brief them on the matters upon which they have to make decisions. That service is available to them, but they also have a whole host of executive assistants, special assistants, research people and advisers to work with them as a government, to think in their terms and to help ministers make the decisions that they must make on matters of policy.
I think that this also applies to the rest of us, Mr. Chairman. We are all entitled to the objective, impartial kind of research material that we can get from the library. But we are also entitled to have people in the research field working with us in our various groups, understanding our approach, looking for the kind of things that will help us solve problems, that will help us come to decisions in the light of the particular philosophies that the members of the various parties in this house have. That is not contrary to the Prime Minister's suggestion.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
I think we all agree that this money must not be used for party purposes; it must not be used for the organizational work of the parties outside the house. I am sure he will agree with me 100 per cent that inside the house our parties and the cut and thrust of debate between the parties form the very essence of parliament. We need, therefore, that kind of research which will inform and strengthen us along the lines of the positions we in the various parties take.
I am pleading, although no doubt the hon. member for York South would be doing so in more biting language, for that change which we hope will come some time in the future. I shall have to settle for the Prime Minister's assurance that this is but the beginning, that once this kind of money shows up in the estimates it will be possible to enlarge the estimates and go farther in future years.
There is a particular angle to this matter that concerns me, concerns my leader and concerns most hon. members. We are concerned that the amount of money being provided is so small that unless something is done about the Joe staff, if I may put it that way,
November 15, 1968

in our leader's office and unless something is done to help our leader to cope with his ordinary day to day work, this money may be used to cover just that situation. For a good many years my office has been opposite my party leader's office, and I have a pretty good idea of what goes on in that office. I have seen it operating under two or three different leaders. It seems that it is the nature of the leader's office, and no doubt the Prime Minister is discovering this, that a particularly heavy work load comes into it. The correspondence is unimaginably heavy. A great deal of mail comes to the leader of the party, and that it is impossible for one person and one secretary to handle it is incontrovertible.
What must our leader do, Mr. Chairman. He has to persuade good people, people with university degrees and with experience who could get jobs elsewhere at higher pay, to come and work for him in that office, either at minimal rates of pay that the party provides from the outside or at rates of pay that are below those provided for executive assistants. As a result our leader has quite a few helpers, it is true; some of them are volunteers and some of them are from the outside. But he needs these people just to do the day to day Joe work. There is a very real danger that this money, which I understand in a full year would be only $35,000, much less than that for this year, will be absorbed to cover our leader's Joe work and that we shall not obtain from it what is wanted, namely, research work to assist hon. members to be better informed. That danger exists in a very real way and will continue to exist until this other problem has been dealt with satisfactorily.
I shall spend no further time on this matter, since it is still being negotiated. The leader of our party was greatly concerned when the proposal came from the Prime Minister. He was led to believe that this money was to be used to pay the salaries of people who would be capable of doing active research work. It ought not to be used merely to pay for the day to day work in the leader's office. We are all to be covered by this small amount of money. Hon. members who sit in the second, third, fourth and fifth rows and who need research assistance of the kind the Prime Minister is talking about just will not obtain it. I therefore think that the Prime Minister's initial gesture might have been considerably expanded.
I think hon. members ought to be told how much money is being spent on each of the
Supply-Legislature
smaller parties, how much is being spent on the official opposition, how much is being spent in enlarging the Prime Minister's office staff and the staff that is looking after his Joe work, his research work and all the rest of it. If we have that information we may better judge how generous is this gesture toward the third and fourth parties in this house.
In addition to the ordinary work load hon. members have as such because of matters that come to their offices, the steady run of human problems, and in addition to the ordinary correspondence they must deal with, they are often asked to help in other ways. I suppose I have helped to write hundreds of graduate theses in the quarter century I have been here. Every week young people approach me with requests of that kind. I think this is a legitimate request for students across this country to make of their members of parliament. That is part of the job.
On top of all this work there is our work in committees. I agree with the proposal that we make more use of our committees. I think we must consider attaching some kind of research staff to the committees themselves. I do not say we must go to the extent they have in the United States. All those who have been down there know how lavish they are with money for research purposes. The point is that when we are asking for all these things we are not asking for public funds to be squandered. We are trying to make sure that we get better value for the money we already spend on the institution known as parliament and on having members of parliament here.
We are all terribly aware of the work load that goes with parliament. I will not be divulging caucus secrets when I say that some time ago, at one of our caucuses, we had an outsider in who pleaded for something to be done. The retort was made, "Why don't you get yourself elected to parliament?". One of our new members who felt overworked already immediately replied, "The job isn't what it's cracked up to be."
I believe a good many new hon. members are finding the work load heavy. But we are here because we like it. We like what we are able to do. Some of us like it so much that we hope to stay here forever-if we are allowed to. We have an important job to do for the people of Canada and it is by no means a mistake to ask for public funds to be used to support that work and see it is done well.

We shall certainly vote for item 20a, the item we are in effect now discussing. We hope that this is only a beginning toward the provision of proper and adequate assistance to members of parliament generally.

Mr. Chairman, I want first of all to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for having fulfilled a promise made in the Speech from the Throne, to the effect that the Opposition parties would receive some help from the government in order to reach maximum efficiency.
The Prime Minister has just repeated that, to ensure maximum efficiency to the opposition parties and their leaders, supplementary estimates are presented today, which will help them considerably to fulfil their duties more actively and more efficiently than in the past.
I note in passing that this initiative of the government, probably conceived by the Prime Minister himself is due to the fact that, having for such a long time himself opposed any government in Canada, he has understood the importance of an active opposition. I knew him when he was active. In 1944-quite some time ago-he went around for the C.C.F. with Mrs. Therese Casgrain. He even came to Rouyn-Noranda and I went to hear him speak during the provincial elections of 1944.
The Prime Minister, therefore, knows what he is talking about when he speaks of the important role the opposition can play in a democratic parliament.
Mr. Chairman, in addition to the amounts the Prime Minister or the government suggests should be paid the leaders of the parties of the opposition to organize a research department, we must also consider the matter brought up by the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to the effect that those amounts are not made available only to the leaders of the parties, although the leaders are formally mentioned.
The fact is that, in any political party, there is some form of discipline and I believe the leader is the one who represents the whole party. Just as the Prime Minister represents the whole Liberal party, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) represents Conservative members as a group, and the leader in parliament of the New Democratic party represents the socialist members

of this house, and I feel I represent the members of the Ralliement Creditiste group.
This means, Mr. Chairman, that the help we receive belongs of necessity to our respective deputations. In my case, if we increase the staff assigned to research or such work as is absolutely essential, that staff will be available to our whole party. I believe the same applies to the other parties.
Now, there is another point to which the government or the Prime Minister must give much attention, and that is office facilities. At the present time, the situation is absolutely unbearable. In my own case, for instance, four employees share a single office about the size of a handkerchief, which is hardly satisfactory. The whip of the Liberal party is looking at me and signalling that this is a serious problem. He is, in fact, fully aware of the situation in which I find myself. More space must be found for the opposition parties.
Some minister have five, six or seven offices in the centre block, even though they have huge offices in their respective department buildings. Two sets of offices are provided for the ministers and for their parliamentary secretaries, whereas the opposition parties are in a strait jacket. They find it absolutely impossible to get any co-operation from the government. The opposition parties must be given more office space.
Another point which I want to bring to the attention of the house is that the right hon. Prime Minister has mentioned in the Speech from the Throne and repeated in this house this very afternoon that the public must realise the important role of the opposition in parliament. There is rather a contrast between that and what was said before the election, for example. The public was then told: Vote for the government if you want to get anything. They are urged to vote for the party in power, but no one knows which party will be in power. We often hear that.
Today, I think this clearly demonstrates the position and the importance of an efficient opposition which will preserve our democratic principles. That means that a member of the opposition must receive the same treatment as a member of the party in power, if we really want justice to prevail in the administration of public affairs.
I think that the fine initiative of the Prime Minister confirms the importance of an efficient opposition, well informed and prepared to play its part as a critic of a responsible government. Mr. Chairman, this is an
November 15, 1968

essential condition so that the public may be aware of the importance of the opposition to the government.
Here is another point on which I wish to draw the attention of the Prime Minister. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said a while ago, an amount of $35,000 is allotted to the small parties of the opposition and $125,000 to the main opposition party. As for ideas, that party is smaller than the others, but it has more members than ours, I admit it.
We are bound by those recommendations which we feel constitute a first step towards helping the small parties of the opposition. Needless to say, eventually that will not be sufficient, because like every other minister or the Prime Minister himself we have more work than we can do. What staff does the Prime Minister have? A staff of 28 people: writers who prepare the speeches for the ministers and dozens of researchers, in short a numerous personnel.
Let us not forget, Mr. Chairman that although the right hon. Prime Minister indicates that it is not so, I believe he needs that staff to fulfil his duties properly and to enable the government to discharge its responsibilities. I am not criticizing the size of the staff, but I do want to point out what our situation is compared to that of the government.
The amounts we accept are just a start. They will help us, there is no doubt about it, to better fulfil our duties. They will help not only all the members of the Ralliement Creditiste, but their leader as well.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, the opposition might also play an efficient role in another field. I have already called the Prime Minister's attention to that matter by writing to him personally. It deals with transport facilities for the leaders of the various parties. For instance, we are invited to go to western Canada to speak before university students about the role of a parliamentarian or any other matter of public interest, and not to play politics, although that can be done. The Prime Minister is not above doing it at times; I have the right to do it too just like the leaders of the other opposition parties.
I asked the Prime Minister that a pass valid on Air Canada flights be delivered to the four federal political leaders. So far the Prime Minister does not need a pass, because he has his private plane, that is the government plane. The Leader of the Opposition has
Supply-Legislature
a pass which enables him to travel on all Air Canada routes from the Atlantic to the Pacific, whereas the leader of the New Democratic party and the leader of the Ralliement Creditiste do not have such a pass. As far as I am concerned, I have a pass which allows me to go home to Rouyn once a week. All hon. members have one. I am not asking that a pass be delivered to all hon. members, but the fact remains that there are two political leaders of parties now represented in parliament who do not have that pass.
The management of Air Canada has not even found it appropriate to answer me when I requested one and I say that the Prime Minister did not answer me either. Yet, he has received a personal letter from me on that matter.
When we have to pay such transportation costs, it means spending a considerable amount of money which we certainly cannot always take out of our own pocket. Sometimes people invite us and send us an airplane pass, so that we have nothing to pay. It seems to me that if the leaders of the New Democratic party and the Ralliement Creditiste had a pass enabling them to travel from eastern to western Canada, when they are invited to perform official functions, when they are invited by social clubs, chambers of commerce, municipal authorities, or to attend regional conventions of various organizations, Air Canada or the Canadian government would not be poorer for that.
Mr. Chairman, I draw the Prime Minister's attention on that point, to see whether it might be possible to add to both the two small items the amounts requested by the representatives of the New Democratic party and of the Ralliement Creditiste for the leaders, so that they are provided the same facilities as the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition to travel across country.
Mr. Chairman, before concluding my remarks, I want to thank sincerely the Prime Minister for his initiative. I commend him for having fulfilled a promise made in the Speech from the Throne. I think that the supplementary estimates will assist the members in giving a better service to their constituents, while enabling them to discharge their parliamentary duties even better. Thus the Canadian people whom we represent here in the House of Commons will be better served.

Mr. Chairman, I would like first to congratulate the right, hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for this initiative which, I think, constitutes a step forward in

November 15, 1968
Supply-Legislature
the modernization of our parliamentary system. In my opinion, it was advisable to recognize the greater work-load of the party leaders and the additional credits which will be voted will serve to increase their staff. It is a very wise move. However, I hope it will be also followed by another measure long overdue and most important which would improve the services enjoyed by the hon. members.
You will agree with me, Mr. Chairman, that the role of the State, in our political society, is becoming increasingly important. We can expect it to grow apace. The complexity of public administration saddles the hon. members with new and extremely heavy obligations.
The people want their M.P. to fulfil his obligations as a legislator in Ottawa, but they also want him to be present in his riding to provide for all local needs. This is now practically impossible because of the evolution of our parliamentary system.
In view of this, it is advisable to provide members on both the government and opposition sides with services to enable them to fulfil their new responsibilities as well as their duties in the house and in their riding.
I think that, in view of these new needs, we should establish without delay secretariats in the ridings to assist each member with his work on behalf of his constituents. It is true-as pointed out earlier

that there is a staff to serve members, particularly in the library; this staff helps members in the preparation of their work and provides them with guidance in their research.
However, as a result of the evolution of parliamentary procedure-we now have to work practically 11 months a year in Ottawa. A member cannot be active here 11 months a year and make a useful contribution to the proceedings of the House of Commons, while keeping informed of the events in his constituency, in order to answer all the requests of his constituents and professional or social organizations. All that increasingly requires that a member should conduct forums, inform the public of the various political trends and attend social functions, especially those which stimulate the political activity and thought of his electors.
Now, I believe that it is extremely important that we should obtain as soon as possible some help in our constituencies, at least to enable the member, to be represented in order to assure some permanent cohesion between the aspirations of the people or the
[Mr. Ouellet.l
electors of a constituency and the policies applied and passed in Ottawa.
Mr. Chairman, I think we should provide a supplementary allowance to cover the costs involved in hiring a secretary in the riding, as well as renting premises and paying for long-distance telephone calls, because you know that the representatives of rural districts are often compelled to make long-distance calls from one locality to another and this is very expensive indeed. I do not see why a member who has an office in his riding could not have a direct line linking him with the various government departments.
Before concluding my remarks, I would like to deal with another matter. This has already been raised earlier in the day by the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) who is in favour of granting a permanent pass on Air Canada aircrafts to the leaders of the parties. I agree with that. I think this should have been done a long time ago.
Still, I should like to put the following question: if, in the early days of confederation, it was considered advisable to give Canadian members a pass on the railroad, I wonder why, today, considering the evolution in transportation and modern techniques which allow more travel by planes than by railway, the members of parliament could not be given passes on Air Canada planes, just as members were given passes on the trains in the early days of confederation.

Mr. Chairman, when the house took recess at one o'clock, I was saying that it was imperative that members of parliament have access to modern means of transportation and communication.
Years ago, through a legislative measure, parliament granted railway passes to its members. In this age of speed, it would be proper, I feel, to give the members special passes on Canadian airlines. The frequent use of planes for travel is now recognized and accepted by everyone.
Indeed, all the members of this house can travel by plane once a week between their respective ridings and Ottawa. To my mind, it was essential that this principle be recognized. It is especially handy in the case of those members who come from the Maritimes and the western provinces.
However, it should now be recognized that the members who are called upon to vote ever increasing amounts each year for the administration and the legislation of their country, should be able to travel quickly across the country to better know it and, in particular, to study at close range the problems they are called upon to solve.
I recognize that granting permanent passes to all the members of this house on Canadian airlines may cause those companies certain difficulties, but surely some way could be found to allow all the members who so wish to move about rapidly from one end of the country to the other, at least two or three times a year.
Mr. Chairman, I see magnanimity in the attitude of the leaders of the parties who will receive additional amount to help them in their work; I find them magnanimous in the fact that they are willing to share these amounts and this additional help with the members of their parties. But to me, this is not a solution. The needs of the party leaders have been recognized, and assistance is being given to them. They are now provided with extra sums of money so as to fulfil their

November 15, 1968
Supply-Legislature
responsibilities more efficiently. I do not think we should expect them to share those funds with the members of their parties. We must find right now some means of assisting all the members. To this end, I suggest first that the research personnel in the library of parliament should be increased; secondly, every member should be allowed to establish a secretariat in his own constituency. This is, I think, one of the most urgent and pressing needs if the members must continue to play a useful and efficient part in their constituency.
Finally, I think it should be possible for the members to travel about in this country in a swift, efficient and modern way, without having to spend fantastic amounts of money.
Those recommendations should be accepted as quickly as possible so as to render the members' work more effective, in the interest of the Canadian people.
Before closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to a question directed to the Speaker on October 31 last by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) with regard to the translation situation in the committees.
Mr. Speaker, with his great kindness, had accepted to consider the matter and he had said:
I would ask him to wait a few days to give me the opportunity to study the situation a little more closely and then I may be in a position to make a statement in the house-[DOT]
on this subject.
We know the tremendous difficulties encountered with regard to the translation of the evidence of the committees of the house, and if we refer to the report of the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), dated March 31, 1967, we see that the workload of the Canadian government translators is unbelievable and that the number of words and pages translated has tremendously increased during the last few years. This does not only apply to translation but also to interpretation.
I should like to suggest that we might go back to a practice which existed in the early 40's assigning to the House of Commons translators who would exclusively look after the translation of the Debates of the House of Commons and the proceedings of the committees. I think that we are now asking too much from the translation staff, and, to that end, I should like to quote part of the report of the Secretary of State.
Additional to the requirements of parliament, assistance was provided (by the interpretation services) to departments, crown corporations, royal commissions and similar bodies in Ottawa, elsewhere in Canada and abroad.

This means that often, when there is an urgent need for documents and material which have been submitted to one of the committees, unfortunately there are no translators available to do the work and to deliver simultaneously to the members and the public the texts in French and in English. This is a situation which, in my opinion, should be corrected as quickly as possible and I suggest with great deference that the Chair consider the advisability of assigning a staff of translators exclusively concerned with the business of the House of Commons and the committees.
