speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the quiet retreat of the House of Commons on a Friday afternoon there is an excellent opportunity to make some comments on item 20 which deals with the House of Commons itself and to make some reference to the supplementary estimates which were passed. When all over the world today we see signs of violence and the desire of people to change their way of life by sudden and bloody means rather than by the infinite processes which democracy has made available to us, I think it is a good thing to take a minute or two to reflect on what we are, what we do and what we should be able to do. I do this in the full knowledge of the fact that the committee on procedure will be reporting by order of the house on December 1 and I do not intend, except indirectly, to infringe on what I hope will be a very useful and meaningful debate at that time.
I direct my remarks more particularly to the backbenchers opposite. I have been trying to incite a revolt over there for some time without too great a measure of success so far. With regard to the role of the backbencher, hon. members opposite must have been filled with jealousy and some admiration by the very useful and spectacular performance by the six members from Newfoundland who sit on the "right" side of the house and who were able to mount a concerted, effective and useful attack against the very unfair removal of Newfoundland's most necessary passenger train service. It did not take a great deal of time and it was done usefully and objectively. The hon. members spoke with eloquence and in an articulate way brought forward to this house and through this house to the country a very serious and urgent problem. I think they are entitled to the commendation of the people of this country and members of this house
November IS, 1968

for demonstrating that it is possible to do so. I am confident that hon. members opposite must be very frustrated by the inhibitions that prevent them from emulating the kind of presentation the house saw when the members from Newfoundland put forward their arguments last week.
There are very eminent authorities for this sort of action. I am going to try to be as objective as I can, but I should like to Quote some authorities to show the unfortunate predisposition of members of the Liberal party to fail, even in opposition, to take the independent stand they should. I have some quotations here which I will read and possibly hon. members will recognize the source later. All of them come from one article. The first one reads as follows:
There Is not remaining in this party (Liberal) one single man for whom principles mean more than power.
The next one reads:
One finds among the old guard the same brutal cynicism.
Another one reads:
I am only concerned with the anti-democratic reflexes of spineless Liberal herd.
Those are not my words, Mr. Chairman. I would not dream of saying that. Farther on I read:
I would have to point out in strongest terms the autocracy of the Liberal structure and the cowardice of its members.
I have never seen, in all my examination of politics, so degrading a spectacle as that of all these Liberals turning their coats in unison with their chief, when they saw a chance to take power.
Those are sad words, Mr. Chairman. And again:
-where was there a single well-known Liberal to stand up for the constitution of the party, to raise his voice against dictation by the leader, to question his authority thus to commit the party?
Since the present Prime Minister, Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau, used these words in 1963 so effectively and truthfully, I wonder how many backbenchers there are sitting opposite me who would like to say the same thing but who, because of the description which has been given of them, do not dare do so.
Having thus established a foundation which I hope will be continued, I believe this issue becomes one with which we must all be concerned and upon which will be predicated not necessarily the survival of this house-I am not one of those who feel that this institution may be threatened-but the shape in
Supply-Legislature
which it will survive. Its opportunities to make a useful contribution, not only to preserve but to restructure and improve our society, depend on what we do with it and what use we make of the power and authority which it has.
Not long ago I read a very interesting book by Mr. Humphrey Berkeley, a former British member of parliament who belonged to the Tory party. He is no longer a member now. The book is called, "The Power Of The Prime Minister". In it he points out very succinctly the rising power of the prime minister and the addition to the structure of the prime minister's office. He points out the frightful consequences which might well occur as a result.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Berkeley was a very progressive member of parliament. It was he who sponsored and brought forward in the United Kingdom the legislation which was eventually passed dealing with acts of gross indecency. Whether or not one believes in his views, it is at least to his credit that he was able to do this as a private member. He was also very prominent in trying to help the government and parliament to secure reforms in connection with the abolition of capital punishment and changes and reforms in the divorce law.
In his book he points out how slowly, step by step and stage by stage over a period of years, power flowed from the House of Commons into the hands of the government and since then has come to rest almost exclusively upon the shoulders of the prime minister. Of course he makes certain proposals as to how this can be changed. I will not go into them, but here is a man with six years of practical experience in the House of Commons in the United Kingdom who challenged the effectiveness of the rota system in the question period in the English House of Commons. I think anyone who reads Mr. Berkeley's book will see precisely what this government and the Prime Minister are attempting to do and will then conclude that the opposition has indeed been wise and sensible in the attitude it has taken that this change cannot be made. While there may be room for some alteration in the question period, it cannot and must not be done in the way the Prime Minister is attempting to do it but must be done through the process of discussion and reaching a consensus.

November 15, 1968
Supply-Legislature
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
If I had the time, Mr. Chairman, I could take the committee stage by stage, act by act, through the legislative process which we have undergone in this country. Even at this session the major bills which have been passed have all resulted in a further stripping away of power from this House of Commons and giving it to the government. The Canadian National financing bill contained nine clauses giving the Governor General in Council the power to do things which normally would only be the prerogative of this parliament. I recognize it is essential for the proper functioning of the democratic process to give certain powers from time to time to the government. We have seen this happen in bill after bill, session after session. I believe the major points on which the opposition took issue with the government in connection with the farm credit legislation which was passed this session had to do with those areas where power was given to the government to fix the interest rates which would be applied to farmers of this country in an arbitrary fashion. I believe an examination of all legislation passed would show this to be the case.
I have already indicated that to some extent this is necessary. However, to the extent that it is necessary, it is even more essential that we must retain within the four corners of this chamber the independent right to challenge the government when from time to time the government is wrong. The only way we can have that independent right is when backbenchers on the government side and other members have the intestinal fortitude it takes to challenge the government when the government is wrong. There is no doubt that this is going to happen very frequently in the next four years. We must retain within the four corners of this chamber the right to challenge the government, the right to compel the government to give an accounting. We are not here simply to say: Ready, aye ready, pass your legislation; we will restrict ourselves to a feeble protest. Far more than that must be the essential requirement to retain an effective and useful parliamentary system
There are many ways in which this tendency is shown. There is excessive secrecy. There is no doubt that this government has gone far beyond the action it needs to take in order to preserve certain minimum requirements of secrecy. Certainly no one would dare disagree with the right of the Prime Minister to restrict his cabinet ministers in their utterances

so that they will not reveal what has taken place within the secrecy of the privy council chamber. However, the government has gone much beyond that. I say that because this fact is demonstrated in the house day after day when members on the opposition side attempt to secure from the government the facts which they must have if they are going to discharge their duties. These attempts are stone-walled. We get answers but they say nothing. We get statements but they have nothing of fact or consequence included in them. I believe this is well established.
I have here a very interesting article which appeared in this morning's Montreal Gazette written by Gordon Pape. The article is concerned with the problems and difficulties of government. While it is lengthy, the author has only had the space to touch upon a few of these. I should like to refer to the paragraph dealing with excessive secrecy in government:
There was nothing terribly unusual about Mr. Trudeau's edict last summer that cabinet and caucus sessions should be kept secret. Almost every new party leader has, on taking office, made similar statements.
What was unusual was the zeal with which official Ottawa reacted to the statements. Civil servants, many of whom tend to be timid with the pressit is difficult to understand that statement.
-to begin with, have used the Prime Minister's warnings as an excuse to clam up. Some cabinet ministers have become wary with newsmen-
How could they?
-even about matters having to do only with their own departments.
The over-all effect has been to stifle the news flow out of Ottawa to some degree, and to lessen rather than increase public debate on issues up for government scrutiny.
This is the essential reason why there must be complete freedom in the necessary flow of information from the government. This flow of information is necessary in order that members of the opposition may exercise their prerogative of acting for the millions of people who sent them here to challenge the government from time to time and ask the government for the facts. Only in the broad light of publicity are the processes of democracy useful and effective.
This brings me to the last point I want to make. I know there are other members who are most anxious to make their own contribution to the debate on this item. I should like to refer to the extent to which the usefulness of this institution is, in a way, being impaired
November 15, 1968

by the emergence of a new media of reporting. I have no great complaints with the press as a whole. If you manage to read enough newspapers or if you read the same newspaper long enough, you get a fairly balanced diet. It may well be that the people who do not look below the headlines may not find this to be the case. However, if the opinion makers read enough newspapers, I think one can obtain some balance and enough of the facts to know what is going on here and what are the issues.
In recent years a completely new element has been introduced through the media of radio and television reporting. I believe that this and other parliaments must soon come to some decision about how we are going to deal with it. Here we have a situation where members of this house-cabinet ministers, leading members of the opposition parties and backbenchers on both sides-have lavished loving care and objectivity in putting together a speech dealing with a current public issue. The speech is delivered in the house or a question may be asked and answered in the house. Then, outside the doors of this chamber members are met with microphones and cameras and are expected to compress within the limited time of 30 or 60 seconds a complete answer. The result may be a distortion of what has been said in the speech. I am not being critical of the people who ask for these statements. It is a fact of life that this media is here and is not going to go away. Hopefully, we are not going to go away either, so we have to bring these two facts together.
We have seen an illustration of this in a somewhat different fashion when the right hon. Prime Minister saw fit to discuss certain issues in a meeting with students at Kingston. In doing so I think he has created a great deal of confusion and a great many problems for some people in the country and for some of those who represent the country.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
When we first come to Ottawa, Mr. Chairman, and go into the office of the Clerk to take the oath of office I think we must leave outside the door of his office some of our private life. When we go a step farther up the ladder and are called to Government House and there sworn to the privy council, we leave outside the front door of the Governor General's house a great deal more of our private life. If we become prime minister-and I use the word "we" very loosely, Mr. Chairman-I think it becomes very difficult indeed
Supply-Legislature
to retain much of our private life. I do not care how valid the reason or how good the intention, the person who has the honour to hold the first citizenship of this land and be prime minister must understand that he cannot divide himself into a personal self and a public self. When he appears on the public platform or before the television cameras he cannot say anything other than as prime minister of the country. When that fact is recognized, Mr. Chairman, I hope it will make somewhat easier the task of the prime minister's colleagues who sit on the same side of the house as he, as well as all of us in the house, who wish to see the affairs of this country properly and well conducted.
In any event, the time has now come for us to have a good hard look at the question of television and radio coverage of our proceedings. Are we going to let cameras in here? Like the camel and the Arab, the camel is just outside and beginning to get its nose through the door. Are we going to let it proceed in the hit and miss fashion that we have seen existing in the past?
I for one, Mr. Chairman, will be quite honest and say that I have had strong objections, and I still have, to this kind of coverage, but I am beginning to wonder whether those objections are valid any longer. If we are going to be able to portray to the people of this country and to the world a fair representation, in terms of balance, of what: takes place here, then must we not consider approaching the question in a proper and a scientific way?
I do not think that we in this chamber alone can make the rules, though certainly we must have the right of veto. However, I do suggest-and I throw this out as a hint and hope that other hon. members will have something to contribute to it-that before too long a time has elapsed we should get together a group that would include members of this house, members of the other place, some of the chief representatives of the media and see whether or not it is possible to work out a way by which a fair and accurate representation of what takes place in this house from day to day can be presented to the people instead, as I say, of the hit and miss method we are following at the present time.
To me, Mr. Chairman, the securing of ways and means to bring this about represents the greatest difficulty. If the Lord would consent to come down and act as censor and edit the tape, then we might well be able to work out this problem. I was in the United Kingdom

November 15, 1968
Supply-Legislature
last February, and as most hon. members know the British parliament has been tooling with this same question. The House of Commons rejected it. The House of Lords did allow cameras into the chamber on an experimental basis for one debate. This was put on tape and there was a selective showing for those whose hearts were strong enough to stand it. In typical British fashion this debate of noble lords and ladies centred around Sunday sport, on whether or not they should play cricket on Sunday, hold horse races and so on. I must say the debate was not too exciting, but the screening showed two speakers from either side, two from the government and two from the Conservative side. I did not stay to see the showing any longer, but an attempt was made to represent fairly what did take place. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was there and he did indicate he hoped the film would be brought back so as to add support for his campaign to have the Senate abolished.
But seriously, Mr. Chairman, we must wait no longer in facing up to this problem and deciding how to deal with it. Bearing in mind the quite unfair and improper campaigns of vilification that have gone on against many democratic institutions all over the world, the time has now come for us to secure some way of ensuring that what goes on in this place is accurately and properly portrayed to the people of Canada. I say this, Mr. Chairman, because the time may well come when we want in the savings bank of good will the greatest possible fund of understanding and appreciation of what is essential to the survival of this country. Somehow the members in this chamber must secure a distillation of the united wisdom of all the people they represent so that when the occasion arises, as it will from time to time, this wisdom may be set against the government and the will of the people will prevail.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to comment very much on what the hon. member for Peace River had to say except to say that in essence his speech was a forerunner of the one that will follow in the debate on the report of the procedure committee. This committee has been engaged in its occupation for a long time, most of that time without the presence of the hon. member for Peace River. On the whole it seems to me that it would be advisable and desirable to let the committee complete its deliberations without opening up a debate on the question of procedure. Therefore, if I do not comment 
on some of the points he raised at this time my silence does not indicate agreement in any sense with what he said, but rather that I think we should wait for the procedure committee to report and deal with the subject matter then.

I believe the member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) has studied the matter seriously and his suggestions, especially with regard to the translation of the Hansard and the committee reports prove it. I should like to advise the house that later today it will have the opportunity to adopt a motion authorizing an experience with regard to the committees of the house.
As the members know, we have simultaneous translation in the committees, and the officials of the House, have suggested that it might be possible to get a written translation of that interpretation with the original text, as we do in the case of new bills. Thus, we could get the committee reports within a few days of the sittings of the committees instead of a few weeks as is now the case.
I believe also that the house might be willing to pass unanimously this afternoon, a motion which would allow us to adopt that procedure on an experimental basis from now until the Christmas recess.
The hon. member for Papineau, also mentioned secretaries in the ridings and he told us that it is the practice now in Quebec to make these facilities available to the members of the provincial legislature and also to grant them travelling expenses everywhere in Canada as well as other benefits so as to help them better fulfil their duty.
Therefore, I should like to suggest that it might be possible, in the second half of this session, to appoint a committee consisting of hon. members representing all the parties in the house, to study an increase in the staff and an improvement in the working conditions of the hon. members, so that they may better perform their task which consists mainly in representing their voters, reviewing legislation and legislating in the best interests of the Canadian people.
I will also discuss this with my colleagues and the leaders of the other parties in the house to arrive perhaps at a formula which will allow us, in other instances, to consider the working conditions of the members with a view to improving them.
And just to reassure the back-benchers of our party, we admit that we have granted
November 15, 1968

opportunities to the opposition. It is first of all an opportunity for the leaders of the other parties.
We are also fully aware of the problems faced by the members and we do intend to solve them.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to follow the argument advanced by the President of the Privy Council. After listening to the hon. member for Peace River speak about parliament I thought I might refer to several matters. He pointed out that there had been a great change over a period of years in the power and authority of the Prime Minister, a weakening in the power of parliament itself, and particularly in the power of backbenchers.
Throughout the years one of my objectives has been to do everything I could to bring about a full and complete participation, within the limits of parliamentary time, for those hon. members who, elected for the first or second time to the House of Commons, remain backbenchers. I have found from experience that their contributions mean most in giving parliament new hope, new idealism and a new concept of the needs of their generation. Ever since the first world war the trend has certainly been away from the backbencher. The trend in Canada has been similar to that in the United Kingdom. The centralization of power in the Prime Minister, and indirectly but powerfully in the cabinet, has brought about a condition that is not healthy to the concept of the House of Commons being the house of the common people.
In setting forth his views the hon. gentle-maP. re^erre<^ to the radio and television facilities that are now immediately available in the foyer of the House of Commons. There must be a good reason for this to have happened. My analysis of the change that has been brought about is that more and more the press gives less and less space to the speeches made by hon. members in the House of Commons. I recognize there is every reason for that. High costs that are ever-rising make it impossible for the press in any event to give anything more than a mere summary of what each hon. member may contribute to the house in his speech. I may be repetitious in advancing these remarks, but I have advanced them before.
I should like to see the press of our country follow the example of the London Times
Supply-Legislature
which daily sets out what took place in the House of Commons and in the House of Lords the day before. A line or two is devoted to each hon. member who spoke and the purport of their views.
Nothing is more discouraging to those serving in parliament than, after having prepared their speeches, to have no one listen to them. Speeches are not listened to unless they are well prepared and show that the midnight oil has been burned. Often a young man or young woman works with dedication to prepare a speech and then finds that there is no mention of it in the press. Hell hath no fury like the failure to mention an hon. member's contribution in the House of Commons.
Hear, hear.

It would not require much space to make possible this suggestion. I should like to see it tried because I think it would raise the standard of debate in the house if newly elected members or backbenchers in making their contributions knew they would find a short summary of their remarks in the press. That is the first suggestion I make.
I think one reason for the tremendous expansion in the television and radio audience is that television and radio each day let the people of Canada know first hand what has happened. When an hon. member is interviewed outside the house he is able to epitomize and summarize in 30 seconds or a minute the embodiment of the argument he has endeavoured to advance. He thereby becomes known to his constituents, to his province, and to the country. Except for the instrumentality of the media there is no effective way for a new hon. member or backbencher to make his presence and his contribution in the house known.
The tremendous centralization of authority has been mentioned. Until 1914 the Prime Minister was the first among equals. Then began a constitutional change. The books on constitutional development that were written between 1875 and 1914 have no application to the parliaments of today. The prime ministers of an earlier period of history were the custodians of the rights of parliament against the crown. The prime minister of today, of this generation, has become more powerful relatively, under the British system of parliament we have adopted, than the President of the United States.

Hear, hear.

November 15, 1968
Supply-Legislature
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)

Mr. Nixon will become president in January. He will find in Congress, that is, in the Senate and the House of Representatives, the opposite party in a majority. Unless the members of Congress decide to make it possible for the presidential system to operate effectively, he will find himself unable to carry out whatever policies he has advocated unless they are generally acceptable. The Prime Minister is in a different position. He can exercise the overwhelming power which derives from his ability to recommend dissolution, a power which places him in the position not of being first among equals but of being first.
The present Prime Minister of Canada made a declaration that he wanted no more leaks from cabinet or from caucus. I cannot criticize that as far as cabinet is concerned. There was a time within the last two or three years when all that was necessary in order to be fully conversant with most of the controversial matters which arose in cabinet was to have half an hour to spare after the cabinet had met. That was wrong. That was dangerous to our system. When the Prime Minister enunciated the principle that there was to be no more of this, he not only enunciated a principle which was proper and fitting but one which was completely consonant with the constitutional responsibility of ministers. In the last few days, however, the fears of yesterday are being disregarded. Ministers are now going here and there making announcements. While this House of Commons is sitting, if an hon. member asks what is the view of the government with reference to statements which are being made, the answer is certainly not one which indicates any endeavour to give an answer.
We have seen an example within the last 48 hours. The Leader of the Opposition, together with other hon. members in all opposition parties, was pressing to find out where this government stands on the subject of NATO- what the Canadian attitude is to be, whether there is to be a change, whether it is intended for Canada to depart from its responsibilities to stand in confrontation against communism through NATO or whether we as Canadians are to adopt a new isolationism whereby, though remaining a member of this organization, we shall not carry a fair and responsible share of the load. We could not get an answer.

One has only to read Hansard in the last few weeks to realize that the period for questions is mainly given to questions, not to answers. We have reached a point at which a question asked is becoming a question unanswered, regardless of its simplicity or the need for an answer. It is true there are some ministers who will give an answer, and I follow the course of thanking them when they do so. There are others who are adopting an attitude of mind which is pretty close to being contemptuous toward those who ask questions.
Hear, hear.

The President of the
Treasury Board, with his experience of parliament and his kindly face, disagrees. When he has been here a little longer he will agree. I always like the affability with which he approaches these problems.
Yesterday we could not get an answer regarding NATO. There was talk, there was uncertainty, there were woolly pronouncements on the subject of NATO. Yet, while parliament asked these questions, 3,000 miles away a minister was giving an international organization information which parliament had the right to know but which parliament was denied. This will not make for an effective House of Commons.
There are, naturally, matters of a secret nature which cannot be revealed. But when the questions were asked yesterday and the day before, and the answers given had all the uncertainty of deception, one cannot expect parliament to enjoy the respect that it should command. We ought to have been given answers. Today, following the effusive frankness of the Minister of National Defence abroad, the Prime Minister gave answers, and by the time he was through I doubt that one Canadian had one certain idea of what this government intends to do with regard to the organization which has preserved our freedom since 1948. In the interests of preserving this institution I implore ministers to see to it that questions are answered.
There are two new ministers from the west, each without portfolio. These two ministers have in the course of the last six weeks recognized that parliament is entitled to information, and I commend them for the manner in which they have answered questions with regard to departmental matters for
November IS, 1968

which they only recently accepted responsibility. This should be the course followed by all ministers.
We do not expect ministers to tell us everything. That would not be human. But after the loose nonsense which was spoken at Queen's and the still looser talk at Halifax about Stalingrad, the Nazis and the like, we are entitled to have answers which are appropriate to questions asked about the defence of Canada, even though, because of the limitations of the need for secrecy, full information cannot be given.
I am glad to see that in the last two or three weeks ministers have to a considerable extent removed the shackles of silence. They are showing less fear than they showed following the declaration of eternal silence for them. I only hope that ministers such as the minister of defence, when he returns to this house, will display the same freedom to speak in the house as he has shown abroad.
I listened to our house leader dealing with the subject of prime ministers and their power. It has been an amazing transition that has taken place. There are few who have ever analysed what is happening in our parliamentary system. With the passing years, the power centre has shifted increasingly to the prime minister. The reason is the acceleration of powers that have come about through the practice of successive prime ministers. The expression "prime minister" is not to be found in Canada's written constitution. The British North America Act makes no reference to it. No one was sworn in as prime minister from 1867 until 1920 at which time Right Hon. Arthur Meighen was sworn in as the first prime minister. Since then it is of interest to note that one or two of those who have been prime minister have not taken the oath as prime minister, because there is no position for which such oath can be taken.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Until 1896 there was no designation of the powers of a prime minister. In 1896 Sir Charles Tupper, in the short period he was in office, decided there should be a declaration as to the authority of the prime minister and an order in council was passed which, in general, has been followed by successive prime ministers from Tupper to Mackenzie King.
The last of these power declarations was by Right Hon. Mackenzie King. Mr. St. Laurent, when he followed as prime minister, did not add to or detract from the powers. When I followed him I made no declaration, and my
Supply-Legislature
information is that neither did Mr. Pearson, nor the present prime minister. Therefore the powers in general are set out in an order in council which Mr. King had passed in 1935 shortly after he took office.
If I might place it on record, sir, it answers many of the queries as to the powers of the prime minister. It says first:
A meeting of a committee of the privy council is at the call of the prime minister and, in his absence, of that of the senior privy councillor, if the president of the council be absent.
The quorum is four, and the order in council sets out:
No submission for approval to the Governor General can be made with a less number than the quorum.
A minister cannot make recommendations to council affecting the discipline of another department.
The prerogative rights of the Prime Minister are the right of dissolution and convocation of parliament, the appointment of privy councillors, of cabinet ministers, of lieutenant governors, of provincial administrators, of the Speaker of the Senate, of the chief justices of all courts, of senators, of subcommittees of council, of treasury board, of the committee of internal economy of the House of Commons, of deputy heads of departments, of the librarians of parliament, of crown appointments in both houses of parliament, and of the Governor General's secretarial staff. I may be wrong in this but my recollection is that Mr. King had this further one added: recommendations in any department.
In other words, the power of the prime minister is an overriding one that knows no challenge. Prime ministers should not make statements off the record outside the house, or in answer to questions, that may give rise to answers that will be prejudicial to the nation, to the people, or lastly to the government. Normally speaking, the average period is some 15 years being a member before becoming prime minister, because the prime minister carries in his person the leadership of the nation. He is the example to the people of the nation, to the youth of the nation and, above all, he must uphold the rights of the institution in which he has the first position; and in saying that I am not forgetting that the Speaker is the First Commoner.
I suggest that we in this house should try out television and see whether it will work. The example that was quoted of what happened in the United Kingdom in the House of Lords, and of the day chosen to test out the

November 15, 1968
Supply-Legislature
efficacy of television, does not convince me in any way that it would not be helpful.
I can tell you, Mr. Chairman, if we had television in this house, not for all day, not for several hours, but with a committee limiting it to 20 minutes per day, we would have no more absenteeism in the house after the first showing of the television across Canada.
I cannot think of anything that to a greater extent would bring about the fullest of attendance than just a daily general survey of the house by a television camera. It would do that which nothing else could possibly achieve.
I hope the government will do everything it can not to appear to push rules down to the house. The President of the Privy Council is an affable and distinguished looking man, but he has developed a complex which is a dangerous one-the idea that he can say to parliament what it is going to do. It was a frightful mistake when this serial presentation of ministers was provided, and it came about when a committee of parliament had been set up and was desirous of bringing about changes. Changes should never be brought about by the autocracy of any minister or by the action of any majority. Changes have got to represent the viewpoint of the house.
Second, in any changes you have in mind remember this: Do not destroy the mission of this house. Some talk of efficiency: "We want parliament to be efficient" has been the cry for 150 years. Parliament is not a joint stock company in which the prime minister is the president of the board of directors, the ministers are directors, and the rest of us are shareholders. Such a concept of parliament will bring about efficiency, as Hitler found and Mussolini found, but what will be lost will be that human element, that desire to co-operate together while differing in detail, to demonstrate that while having strong opinions members are united in one purpose, the pursuance of and the maintenance of freedom.

Let us co-operate together to make this institution, not greater than it has been in the past but the institution that we will defend, rather than join in criticizing at

a time when there is such a contagious attitude in all the western world to criticize these institutions which have preserved our freedom for generations.

I should like to continue for a moment or two with regard to another subject in connection with the House of Commons and its services. This alludes to what we were discussing this morning on the question of research services. I was very gratified indeed to see that a sum of money has been provided for an increase in the research services for the office of the Leader of the Official Opposition and the offices of the leaders of other opposition parties in the house. I should like also to refer to the remarks made by the Prime Minister concerning the research services now available in the library of the House of Commons.
There are some things which might be noted about these services. First of all, as was pointed out very ably this morning by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the services do not include the backbench members on the government side. In fact and in reality they hardly include the back bench members on the other side of the house. These research services are pretty strictly confined to the offices of the leaders of the opposition parties and in fact once they are implemented will not have any real official status.
At this time, although I believe it is apparent to every member of the house, I should like to point out to members how difficult it is in standing committees of the House of Commons, when we examine the government, to have available to us competent assistants in the form of research experts who are capable of guiding us in an intelligent examination of the servants of crown agencies who appear before us. One of the best places to see this phenomenon is in the committee on transport and communications because this committee deals with a subject that is very technical indeed and one which certainly requires a good deal of expertise on the part of members before they can properly come to grips with what is a very complicated and technical subject. If as members of parliament we wished in that committee to examine intelligently let us say the officials of the C.N.R. or, as was the case this morning in respect of the members from Newfoundland, if we wished to examine the new commissioner of the Canadian Transport Commission on the subject of passenger service in Newfoundland, surely we should have available to us through the committee system of the house technical guidance which would enable us at an official level to penetrate the field of administration and examine these people on a competent basis.

Certainly this is the way examinations are carried out in a law court. It is the way the government itself functions through royal commissions and all kinds of other investigations when it wants to find out something and investigate the technicalities of it. This I believe must be a part of the services of the House of Commons if we as backbenchers are to make real progress. I think it must be recognized that within the framework of the House of Commons we are two kinds of people. First of all, we are members of parliament, but in addition to that there are the cabinet ministers who have an administrative function to perform and who have a body of experts who travel with them and assist them whenever they make statements. For our part as members, we have no expertise available to us when we examine the experts whom we must confront each time we have the officials of a department before us during a meeting of a standing committee of the House of Commons. So, when looking at the subject of expanding research, I appeal to the administration today to consider that all of us here in the House of Commons are badly in need of an increased capability built into the committee system which would enable us to perform effectively the work of the standing committees when we examine the estimates and other matters which come before the House of Commons.
I shall not pursue this much further, although I should like to bring out another highlight. When I first came to this house in 1963 the then minister of national defence had promised that he would have established within the House of Commons a committee on national defence. He carried out that promise, so we were the first members of a committee whose function it was generally to look into questions of national defence. We were for the first time faced with the problem of coming to understand the function of a department which was then spending a quarter of the taxes raised from the people of Canada for federal services, namely $1.5 billion. One can readily imagine how difficult it was for a novice in the House of Commons to have any comprehension of what $1.5 billion was, much less how that amount of money could be spent within the framework of a department such as the Department of National Defence which, through tradition, had been very secretive indeed about how its budget was handled and where the money went.

Mr. Chairman, I want to deal today with the subject on which we began discussion this morning and which the Prime Minister led off, namely the subject of increased assistance to members of parliament in the field of research. I do this, not in the almost apologetic way in which I felt the Prime Minister backed into this subject, but because in my opinion, and I think in the opinion of people who have studied the functioning of government and parliament in great detail, it is of the utmost importance that all members of parliament, those in government and opposition, including backbench members on the government side of the house, obtain the kind of assistance which will permit them to do the job required.
The government of Canada is every year dealing with more problems which face the Canadian people. We are spending this year over $10.5 billion. In the last dozen years we have more than doubled the expenditures of the federal government. I am not critical of this; I think we have done no more than we

ought to have done. Indeed I think there are many things which we ought to have dealt with but have not yet considered. It does not surprise me that the staff available to the Prime Minister and members of the cabinet has been increased at a fantastic rate. I am not critical of that.
I think we all recognize that the staff of this Prime Minister has doubled since the government took office. Speaking from memory-and I do not think I am far wrong in saying this-press reports are that there are now some 28 people, or there were a month ago and this is probably out of date now, working in the Prime Minister's office. This is double the number of people working in the office of Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, when he was prime minister.
The Prime Minister has decided-and I am not being critical-to open up what he has called regional desks in his office. The Globe and Mail of November 4 this year lists some of the people who have already been assigned to the task of handling regional desks. There is Mr. David Thompson, who is the regional officer for western Canada. Jean Hache is looking after the regional desk for the mari-times, and Mr. Levasseur is at the moment looking after the Quebec regional desk. He is looking at Ontario candidates for a replacement for that position. I think this is necessary.
As the right hon. member for Prince Albert said a short while ago, the office of the Prime Minister is increasingly important in the decision making of governments of this country. I think it is necessary and I support the increases which have been made. However, the Prime Minister's office is not the only one which has an increase in staff. What is true of the Prime Minister's office is true, on a smaller scale, of every minister. We now have more ministers than this country has ever had. We have ministers and associate ministers. We have ministers without portfolio. We have a whole host of parliamentary secretaries. Each of these has executive assistants, speech writers and public relations officers.

We have a new Department of Manpower and Immigration. We are spending a very substantial amount of money on manpower training, but we need to spend more money on that than we have spent until now because in our increasingly technological age a person who wants to work and who does not have the skills required has virtually no chance of getting any kind of decent wage. Certainly we need to do something very drastic to get rid of rural poverty. I am told by a man whom I consider to be the most knowledgeable expert in the field of agricultural economics in Canada that until recently we gave very little thought to our ARDA programs and to the problems, not of those people who will remain on large farms and who hopefully will be able to make a decent living, but to the problems of those people whose farms will be purchased and who hopefully will move away from the farms on which they have lived for generations.

I want to conclude by quoting just one paragraph from an article which appeared in the winter issue of the Queen's Quarterly for the year 1957. This article is entitled, "Toward a well-informed parliament" and it was written by Mr. Donald Eldon, who was at that time research director of the Progressive Conservative party. I will just read the first paragraph of the article because I think it is one to which the government ought to give some consideration:
Are Canadian politicians well informed? Sound legislation will come out of parliament only if alternative viewpoints and prescriptions for government action are expressed clearly and accurately. The more complex government becomes, the greater is the need for clear talk in parliament. Yet today it is increasingly difficult for the legislator to master the many subjects upon which he must speak and pass judgment, unless he is adequately served by an expert research staff. In an era of complex government there is a danger that only the cabinet, which has direct access to the experts of the civil service, will be well informed. As a result there is grave danger in Canada that the government backbencher and the opposition collectively who do not, generally speaking, have access to as many competent sources of information as the ministers, will become ciphers.
Well Mr. Chairman, 11 years have passed since that article was written. The budget of the Canadian government has doubled since that time. Legislation, such as the Canada Pension Plan, the medicare plan, and the employee training plan, to mention but a few which affect the welfare of every Canadian citizen has been passed. Mr. Chairman, an hon. member who spoke earlier blamed the government for trying to display a kind of superiority complex, a kind of inclination to create an impression that it had a divine right to administer alone the estimates of this country, and he said that it might be an infringement upon the democratic system. This had already been mentioned by previous speakers.
However, we should remember that we all believe in the democratic system. We are convinced that, at a given time, through the democratic process, people choose a government and, under these circumstances, they gave it a majority which does not lead to confusion and does not allow any doubt. However, a government which has received the confidence of the people in our democratic system, still has to perform its duties, to assume its responsibilities, to make decisions and not let these endless proceedings be carried on sometimes indefinitely by people who have some interest in filibustering. There comes a time when the government must put its foot down, so that the people can say to it in the next elections that it has done well, or poorly. But the people will have accomplishments to weigh, analyse and study. However,

if we continue, under the cover of democracy, to chit-chat indefinitely, we will accomplish nothing.
Instead of blaming the government, I feel we should congratulate it for having the courage to assume its responsibilities. Besides, the opposition has every opportunity to criticize; for instance, look at the question period where the opposition absolutely monopolizes the attention of the ministers who are there and that of the government, and the interviews broadcast on the radio, on television, and those published in the newspapers. We know the opposition benefits much more from them than the government, because when it blames the government it makes the headlines. I do not believe the opposition can complain about being muzzled and being unable to exercise its rights as the opposition. On the contrary, it exercises it with zeal.
Someone talked earlier-my remarks are a little disconnected because I am trying to hurry-about putting research facilities at the disposal of the leaders of the opposition parties.
I would like to call the attention of my colleagues to the rather extraordinary research possibilities which exist here in parliament. There is for instance-I am saying that for ordinary members-the parliamentary library. The national library does not have any specialized research staff, but it boasts an outstanding classification system. It includes among other things the catalogues of all the main libraries in Canada. Should a member of parliament, a senator or a minister need a work of reference not available in parliament, he can contact the national library and he will be told where to get it if it is not available at the national library. It is about the same reaction we might have upon hearing the remark I mentioned earlier concerning what I said about the member for Winnppeg North (Mr. Orlikow). Nevertheless it must be recognized that we have a government elected with an unquestionable majority, a great majority, a government to which the nation has given a mandate. They draft their bills, introduce them in the house and give the opposition the opportunity to criticize them or move amendments. Many of these are proposed in parliamentary committees. I know that some opposition members who meet ministers in private make constructive suggestions which are accepted, but a decision must finally be taken and the government assumes its responsibilities, even though, afterwards, it must answer for them to the people.
The hon. member for Peace River added that he would like to keep his right of criticizing the government, of calling it to account. That is perfectly in order and I do not think that he is frustrated of anything. Indeed I think-and that goes for all the opposition- that he has more opportunities to criticize the government than we have ourselves.
We allow ourselves to criticize under certain circumstances and our friends sometimes regret that we do not do it publicly. We do it unobtrusively, because we are not bent on making the headlines; we are not looking for newspaper articles stating that one part of the Liberal caucus is deeply divided against the other. We are trying to solve the problems, but we have no objection when the opposition takes all possible means to criticize the legislation of the government, because we feel that it is a democratic attitude.
However, we should not be grudged what was termed a while ago excessive secrecy and discretion. It is quite obvious that the Liberal party does now wash its dirty linen in public, but does it at home. We should not be compelled to perform a self-examination here in the house, as is done in certain religious orders where public confession takes place. I do not think one can demand those things from us.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said that he wished debates of the house were televised. I know

several members in this house-I for one- who would not be too keen about the idea.
Of course, the member for Prince Albert would try to monopolize the 20 minute period, or perhaps the member for Temis-camingue would try and secure part of it. This would not settle the problem of backbenchers, even though the member for Prince Albert said that it could perhaps help, in discouraging absenteeism. Maybe we could compromise and televise certain debates of parliamentary committees. But as far as discussions of more important questions in this house is concerned, I object. But Mr. Chairman, this is not my main point.
My main purpose in rising now was to make a recommendation to the government and to the right hon. Prime Minister with all the energy I can possibly command.
I think that it was a very good thing to provide the opposition with research services. I agree on that with everyone. However, we should go further. The most urgent priority is to allow all members-those in opposition as well as those in the government-to hire someone to replace him in his riding, whether we call him a secretary or whatever name we want to give him. I think that this is a must for all kinds of reasons.
First, this secretariat could be used as an information centre for the riding. There are many government agencies but not everyone knows where to find them. Not everyone knows how to get in touch with us.
The office of the member is normally a sort of clearing house, an information centre for the distribution of information. However, the member is not there at least five days a week, and some do not even go home on week-ends.
It would be very important to have a representative in the riding in order to serve the public in every respect. This representative could also, sometimes, call the attention of the government on the deficiencies of some services, about which we hear sometimes several weeks or months later when the situation has deteriorated. The people who are on the spot would receive the complaints day after day and could bring them to the attention of their member. This might be used by the opposition as an argument, but it would at least provide some material for the members of the government.
In many cases, this secretary could settle a lot of problems which end up in the office of the members in Ottawa and which he does not have time to settle because, in a very short period of time, the secretary could get
November 15, 1968



used to the job and know where to go so as to settle these cases. Therefore, he would relieve the member of what we might call routine or what my honourable friend called earlier Joe's work, the daily work which anybody can do with no need to refer it to the member.
Under certain circumstances, he could replace the member who is in Ottawa, at official functions, where the mayor, the aider-men, the school board presidents are invited. The secretary of the federal member could go and represent not only the member but also the government. This would relieve the member of parliament from a number of problems that would not end up on his desk, because they would be settled right then and there.
I need not explain, I think, the work of a member of parliament. As a matter of fact, he comes to his office in the morning and sees on his desk a pile of mail. He has to study bills and the briefs that are sent to him from all parts of this country, read his voluminous correspondence, sit on committees, examine carefully reports from previous procedures, run from one committee room to two or three others, eat a quick lunch at noon, attend as often as possible the sittings of the house. He must answer all mail and prepare the interventions he will make in the house and the speeches he will be called upon to deliver before social clubs, commerce chambers or other such organizations. It is materially and physically impossible for him to collect the documents he needs.
Then the riding secretary would unburden us from the administrative work, which would result in our being able to do a better job here with the means available to us. We would be able to study more thoroughly the legislation on which we are called upon to give our opinion, to prepare more carefully our contribution to parliamentary committees, as well as the speeches we have to deliver on occasion here and there. I imagine there are some members who are quite satisfied to have their speeches prepared by others, but I think the majority of the members would prefer to prepare themselves their own speeches and to write them down in their own words and in the way they would like their audience to understand them.
Mr. Chairman, this is the view of my observations. I should like to insist, with my friend the member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and some of my colleagues of the opposition, and tell the right honourable Prime Minister and the government that the first priority, as
Supply-Legislature
far as services are concerned-now that the question of the research personnel for the leaders of the parties of the opposition has been settled-should be to give each members, in his riding, a secretary or assistant- call him what you will-because the amount of work to be done is accumulating at such a dizzy rate that we are swamped by responsibilities and events and we cannot give our electors the services to which they are entitled in view of what the Canadian budget costs them.
I support that recommendation wholeheartedly in the hope that it will be taken into consideration and that journalists will not see in it a deep split between the back-benchers and members of the cabinet.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I like nothing better than a crowded house; I like an expectant audience! I will not follow the example of two hon. members opposite and inflict my fragile, fractured and fragmented French on the house, because I have too much respect for that fine language. I warn my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre that I will not swing in behind him in his crusade against the Senate. He said he wanted to be here forever. I too hope to be here for a long time. Perhaps when I am 74| I shall join his crusade against that illustrious body, but not before then. I live hopefully in hope.
This is the kind of important debate that comes up from time to time in which we all ought to participate. Down through the years people have been concerned about parliamentary institutions. In the present day there are many reasons for thoughtful people to be more concerned than usual about this institution to which we belong.
We are all aware of the complexity and multiplicity of legislation today. In Canada, elections have come with a frequency which has done dreadful things to legislative programs, to order papers, to fiscal years and God knows what else. We are developing, too. an area of government in the field of dominion-provincial relations which is extremely difficult to comprehend because so much of what is decided behind closed doors rather than in the full light of a legislative body. There are times, also, when we are given to too much partisanship in our legislative bodies. I never could believe that the ties of party could be so strong that even on procedural matters there would be a party line. But at times this is a fact.

November 15, 1968
Supply-Legislature
We are sensitive to the fact that in these days all the institutions of the establishment are under fire. It seems that any institution which exists is, in the minds of many people, automatically ready for discard. Change for the sake of change is often the order of the day.
I think we would be most insensitive in this parliament if we believed for a moment that just because it is old and ancient it is bound to survive and command the respect of the people it serves. It is important that we should strive not only to be effective but to appear effective-to appear efficient, to appear relevant, to appear "plugged-in" to the problems and the people about us. It is not unusual for politicians or, as we like to call ourselves, parliamentarians, to be criticized. We are used to that. We are a familiar stereotype. But when the parliamentary institution itself is denigrated and when it begins to lose respect, it becomes a matter for real and genuine concern. The institution must perform the functions for which it is established. The author of one of our great classics in political science was old Bagehot-bigot Bagehot, as we used to call him; but he was a very wise man, nevertheless. This is what he had to say:
The House of Commons needs to be impressive, and impressive it is: but its use resides not in its appearance but in its reality. Its office is not to win power by awing mankind, but to use power in governing mankind.
This, surely, is what we are grappling with when we seek to examine our structures and our procedures. Many interesting things have been said today-many things with which I agree and some with which I disagree. I do not agree with the Prime Minister that the research staff is adequate. I think it is inadequate. May I explain that I think it is inadequate numerically; the people there are doing an excellent job, but there are not enough of them. Many of us who use the services of the research staff with great satisfaction would be glad to use them a great deal more if there were more personnel. I say that the time to expand this service is now.
It is often said that the only people who approve of television in the House of Commons are those who have the physiognomy of a Greek god. I wonder if I am betraying my class when I say I am coming increasingly to the conclusion that we should probably be moving in the right direction if instead of having television off to one side, as is happening now, and the nation being governed in part by television, television should come into

the legislative institution itself. This may be hard on some of us who have long passed the age of beauty, but I think we would have to endure these circumstances. If the hon. gentleman questions that, I thank him heartily for his cheerful disclaimer.
There are in my view some obsolete and obsolescent practices which we must discard for the sake of efficiency. I have never yet made a speech on this subject without talking about voting machines. Imagine what must go on in the minds of the people in the galleries when they hear a vote called. The Speaker says "Bring in the members" and then they hear the bells ringing for as long as an hour and a half or more. They look at the order paper and note that the vote is scheduled for 9.45 or some such hour. Yet we go on with the present silly practice.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Is
the hon. member not aware that we have made some improvement in voting procedure by prescribing that when a vote is set for a specific time the bells must not ring for more than 15 minutes?

That is excellent, a move in the right direction. But I want further improvement to be made, having discovered that since I came here 11 years ago-and that is not a long time compared with the record of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-I have spent the equivalent of 30 sitting days waiting for bells to stop ringing, and though I do not think my time is the most precious in the world I still believe there are better ways of disposing of it.
That is why I would welcome this improvement. If the hon. gentleman could bring about the installation of electronic voting machines we shall have gone even further. We should not be afraid of change. It is necessary to change, though naturally we should not be afraid to retain things of value which have existed for some time.
One thing which concerns me more than anything I have mentioned so far is the growing tendency to by-pass parliament, and I am afraid that the present Prime Minister may be the chief practitioner in this dangerous course. It would be serious if the head of the executive arm should opt out of parliament on important occasions. The Prime Minister of Canada cannot really become a president, our system is not designed in that way. He derives his strength from the public, of course, but he functions only as he commands day in and day out the support of the House of Commons. While ten minute confrontations
November 15, 1968

with students or with Haligonians, or with a few Liberals here and there are very interesting, and make good copy, it is not representative government; it is not direct democracy, either.
The people of Canada are represented in this chamber. Every part of the country is represented here. It is not necessary to have street confrontations to know what Newfoundlanders think of the railway situation. We heard their views eloquently expressed by six able members of this house the other day. It is not necessary to stand on the street corner of Halifax to discover what the people of Atlantic Canada think of the causeway. And no one needs to confront the students in Regina, either, in front of the statue of Louis Riel, or behind it, to know what the people of the west think of the wheat situation. Their representatives here have been telling us succinctly and powerfully.
This is the place where the people are represented. Scattered contacts, however dramatic and pleasing, are no substitute for the continuing relationship between the executive and legislative, which is the very cornerstone of our system. Some of us can remember when a man by the name of Walter Gordon, once a well known figure here, brought in some outside experts. There was a great deal of talk about those outside experts. This is again a matter of public interest inasmuch as the Prime Minister is drawing about him a cadre of experts-150 of them, I believe- who will keep him informed as to the points of view of Canadians everywhere. These are to be the spotters of public opinion.
I do not know what this will do. Naturally, we would like the Prime Minister to see as much as he can, to talk to as many people as he can, and to go to as many parties as he can. That is an excellent thing.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
We like to hear of this sort of thing, but where is the voice of the member of parliament, especially the voice of his own caucus?
The hon. member for Peace River quoted the Montreal Gazette, and to show how ecumenical this party is I am going to quote the following from an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail:
The student mob scene in Regina and the Halifax sidewalk debate on feeding Nazis at Stalingrad may have moved him to reponder Falstaff's advice on discretion and valour-
Yet beyond this maladroitness of technique emerge doubts of principle. First, and perhaps most gravely for democratic statecraft, Mr. Trudeau's compulsion to converse with the people seems often
Supply-Legislature
to by-pass the people's designated spokesmen. A free electorate can readily bear the curbing of an ambitious bureaucracy, but can it tolerate the downgrading of the men it voted in to state its views?
This is a very important question which the Globe and Mail is asking.
The Prime Minister's proposal to set up a network of some 150 hand-picked citizens to advise him on what the people want and think must be regarded as at least a slight to elected Liberal members. No one suspects Mr. Trudeau of wishing to establish a nation-wide ring of more or less secret agents. But one can question the need for such a P.M.'s council when the law and the people's free choice provide for official local spokesmen.
That is what we are here for.
One can ask too whether such shadowy informants can truly reflect the views of the majority of citizens. One can wonder whether they will dare speak frankly to a [DOT] man or a party from whom they might, however distantly or unconsciously, expect some favour-
Here I am in a very embarrassing area. I believe the suggestion is of patronage.
-even the favour of being categorized as one of the 150 insiders.
The the Globe and Mail says:
Finally, one must question still more deeply whether any such elitist scheme to channel opinions is basically democratic. From the leaks about the network's composition, it appears its structure will be priestly and corporatist-the fears and feelings of the masses will be conveyed on high by a hierarchy representing special groups. (As if there were not enough special groups-from the Canadian Labour Congress to the Canadian Manufacturers Association-anxious to advise the Prime Minister.)
Now, that is one aspect-
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Surely.

Was he in the house when his leader spoke to the Prime Minister's suggestion of making funds available for research to opposition members? Was the hon. member here when his leader really served notice on the house that the funds, so far as the official opposition was concerned, might well be used for this type of outside assistance for their own party, the type the hon. member is now suggesting would not be proper for this side of the house?

I think my good friend, and I say this in more than a parliamentary sense, misunderstands me. Of course we do not assume in the Conservative party that all wisdom lies within our caucus. Our leader

would certainly be the kind of person who would be consulting with us; but we in the Conservative party are always ready and eager to consult with people outside it. We would even like to consult with people across the aisle. We are ecumenical in our search to broaden our understanding and knowledge. There is nothing narrow about us. My concern is that those of us who are here to be consulted in a primary sense are being bypassed. However, that will not happen in our party, and I hope it will not happen in the hon. member's party.

speechtext: We often ask for knowledge but we don't often get it from the members over there.

As my house leader points out, very often we try to find out things and you will not really tell us. However, Mr. Chairman, I do not have the time this afternoon to develop either on a philosophic or a pragmatic line this quite important matter.
I think there is a danger of this parliamentary institution being by-passed, being short circuited in this media day of image building, and this could be very serious. I think there are two aspects to what I am trying to suggest. I believe it is very dangerous for the executive to do this. Also it is very much incumbent upon this institution, upon this house, to put itself in such a state of relevancy and effectiveness that it will not be in danger of being scorned and having the public suggest that perhaps in fact it is not functioning as well as it is. I hope my fears are not well grounded, but as I look over what has happened in this country in the last few months there are times when I fear that in a year or two the Canadian people might wonder if majority governments in fact are all that beneficial.

Mr. Chairman, I would have several remarks to make on these votes, especially as regards the organization and staff of the House of Commons, but since they would require a lengthy preparation, I should like to call it five o'clock right away. I will speak when this vote comes up again, as I would not like to split up my speech.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING QUALIFICATION OF VOTERS AND CANDIDATES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-8, to amend the Canada Elections Act (qualifications of voters and candidates).
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-8 is a revival of a bill which was introduced by me in the last parliament. It would provide that Canadian citizenship be a standard qualification for electors and candidates in Canadian federal
November 15, 1968

elections. The motivation for this measure arises not only from a desire to achieve greater justice among those who have chosen Canada as their home, but also to try to do something to cope with the very serious problem that I believe exists with the large number of people resident in Canada and eligible for Canadian citizenship, but who have not applied to become Canadian citizens.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
During the last parliament, through placing a question on the order paper, I found that the estimate of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics extracted from figures in the 1961 census of Canada indicated that there were some 453,441 people at that time who still held citizenship in the countries from which they came, although they had been resident in Canada for more than five years. I since have seen estimates which I believe to be more accurate. One of them was made recently before the standing committee on broadcasting. This estimate placed the figure at about one million people, and my own estimate would place the number at almost one million. It appears to me that while almost 35 per cent of aliens who are eligible for citizenship have not applied, the percentage of eligible British subject immigrants who have not applied is something like 70 per cent. My concern is that not only British subjects but citizens of all countries who have chosen Canada as their new home should be encouraged, through equal treatment in the law, to consider Canadian citizenship as being worth while and to acquire it as quickly as possible.
As I mentioned, this bill was first introduced by me more than two years ago. Since it does seem to have some bearing on citizenship I suppose there might be a suggestion that the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) might have had some hand in this idea, but of course it is very clear that that is not the case, it having been introduced more than two years ago. The bill deals not directly with matters of citizenship but with matters of electoral reform which come under the jurisdiction of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald). I suggest that this proposal, and other proposals for reform of our electoral law, should be studied by a standing committee of this house as soon as possible. I believe the President of the Privy Council has indicated that such a study might take place at the beginning of the new year. I hope therefore that this bill might be referred to
Canada Elections Act
that committee for study of its provisions and the problem out of which it arises. I do not suggest that the proposal I make will solve the problem I have outlined. I do think however, that it would create a more equitable situation in a country which is made up of many different races and of immigrants from many different sources.
Naturally a proposal such as this raises some heated reaction, and I think predictably so. I might share with hon. members some of this reaction which has been both pro and con. One gentleman in Toronto wrote to me, saying in part:
Your name sir is Stanbury, an old country Anglo-Saxon name, yet you have the gall to do this treasonable act toward the greatest tradition in the whole world's history by removing this just preference. I was born in the north of Ireland myself and if I was in good health at over 65 years of age I would sure invite you to a duel.
Another letter from the Toronto area addresses me as "the anti-Britisher" and says: What are you doing about the frogs? The next time I come face to face with your ochre face Stanbury, I will bury you, chicken.
Then this letter from Oakville says:
Jew loving bastard:
We killed many Germans in this last war, not one of them as vile as you.
You are a disgrace to the name you bear. It will be removed from you and your family.
I will censor the next sentence because I think it is too rich even for this place. It ends up with the words "Death to traitors".
I received a letter, too, from something called "The New Right". It refers me to the Bible and says:
As the British people are part of modern Israel, one would do well to read Isaiah, chapter 54, verse 17, and take warning.
Well, perhaps it is significant that I did receive another kind of letter from a Jewish person in Toronto who said:
Bravo!
If we are a truly sovereign nation we should not give preferential treatment to immigrants from any country (except possibly ex-Canadians).
