I refer to another letter which in part reads:
I myself am of Irish nationality with Canadian citizenship so I can speak from personal experience of the views of my English and Irish friends and their absolute rejection of Canadian citizenship as something they don't need. Up until now with the privileges afforded Anglo-Saxon immigrants they didn't, as they put it, need it to participate in the affairs of this country if they felt so inclined.
The fact that they find the country good enough to live in and enjoy the fruits of our high standard of living and yet will not hold up their heads to be counted as Canadians is one hypocrisy that gets me really mad. I do not know if this sense of national feeling is something my Irish heritage brings out in me but I really feel that passiveness in the face of the massive task of giving Canada a feeling of national identity will never get us anywhere.
Another letter from Sarnia says in part:
I wish to commend your action. The present situation in this country does not encourage a total commitment to Canada. The law as it now stands is discriminating against other immigrants while it provides no incentive to the Briton to make himself a true Canadian.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I live in a neighbourhood with a great variety of new Canadians, and I feel sure most of them appreciate the efforts you are making to make all immigrant peoples equal.
I am myself a British immigrant and I know many who fully support the action you are taking.
The only privilege that should be enjoyed by the British immigrant is the privilege of taking out Canadian citizenship. I'm afraid all too few of us do so.
Another letter says in part:
You are so right. No wonder some immigrants feel like second-rate citizens.
To be frank, I am sure most native Canadians were not even aware of this discrimination. I hope they are now.
It may be that the presentation of this bill has made some people more aware of the existence of Canadian citizenship and perhaps has moved them to make application for it. I have here another letter from a constituent who says:
I agree with your change.
He goes on to say:
I believe after two or three years in Canada you should be able to make up your mind to become a Canadian citizen. My family and I are UJC. subjects; we are four, and would like you to tell us how to get the forms to become Canadian citizens.
If my bill has had the effect of making people more aware of the existence of Canadian citizenship and the value of it, and
[Mr. Stanbury.l
has encouraged them to seek it out, I think the presentation of the bill will have been worthwhile. There are of course many people who feel that such a move might be a weakening of our ties with the commonwealth. They point out, as have some hon. members, that this has been traditionally a reciprocal arrangement. I looked into that situation and found that while this might at one time have been the case, at the present time approximately 16 commonwealth countries do not reciprocate in this regard and about seven do.
I cannot venture any opinion on Rhodesia which now considers itself independent, but I suspect that immigrants would not be able to go to Rhodesia, vote and be elected to its legislative assembly, although under our law Premier Ian Smith of Rhodesia could come to this country, live here for a year, be elected to our parliament and entitled to vote in our elections. For that matter, I suppose Lord Thomson of Britain could also.
The arguments against this measure all seem to add up to the fact that people from British countries are necessarily more familiar with our language, assuming it is English, and our laws and customs; but I do not think this is any longer necessarily true. I do not think we can assume that every person coming from a country that is British, or was formerly British, will necessarily be more capable either in language, knowledge of customs or our democratic way of life than a person newly arrived from any other country.
I would like to feel that our laws deal equally with people who have come to Canada to make their home here, no matter from what country they have come. I believe there is more and more acceptance of this idea. When I introduced this bill for the first time, the Toronto Telegram frowned on it, but we seem to be making progress in this regard. In its issue of November 9 it approved the idea and said editorially:
It is to be hoped that no objection to this measure will be raised on the sentimental ground that it weakens the British connection. If there is one British connection which endures, and which is an inalienable Canadian heritage, it is respect for justice and fair play.
Just so no one will think that the Toronto Telegram and the Conservative press are alone in their support of this measure, I should say that the Toronto Star in an editorial of November 7 suggested as follows:
Preferential treatment of British immigrants owes its origins to a time when Canada was the respectful elder child in the British family of nations.
November IS, 19S8

But, while we are still respectful, we have grown up, Our responsibilities are now to our family, and we believe the time has come to place preferential policies on the shelf along with other mementoes of our colonial past.
The Montreal Star has also commented approvingly on this measure. It said in an editorial of November 8:
There probably will be a flurry of protest over indications from Ottawa that people settling in Canada from the United Kingdom may not much longer be entitled to any special privileges. Our colonial heritage is important to some groups across the country, but pride in being a Canadian should be vital.
Its editorial ends by saying:
A country good enough to work in, to live in, year after year, should be worth being a part of.
As one of my correspondents pointed out, my heritage is mostly British. I am proud of it. But I am more proud of my country, Canada. I hope that all people who choose it as their home will be most proud of it, and I hope that by dealing with all people, from whatever country they come, on an equal basis under our laws we will encourage all to become Canadian citizens as quickly as possible and to cherish that right and privilege.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING QUALIFICATION OF VOTERS AND CANDIDATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that this matter has come before the house because it at least opens up the whole question of the franchise in Canada. Lest we be carried away with this idea of treating everybody fairly in Canada-and I congratulate the hon. member who introduced the bill for his very commendable attitude-I think we should not forget one or two very salient facts in this regard. We do not treat our armed forces equally. If you look at the regulations regarding the voting of our armed forces, you will appreciate that it is not a secret ballot at all, because anybody who can count on his fingers can find out who voted how, and where, in respect of any of our Canadian armed forces.
This is something I could put my whole heart behind, namely making sure that those people who have given the most to become Canadian citizens should be afforded equal, if not preferential, treatment. While on this subject I would point out that I know that people who refuse to serve their country in time of war are treated equally with those who do. It is a strange anomaly that in a country where we value freedom so highly those unwilling to serve are entitled to take the highest positions in our land. Not only are they unwilling to serve but are actively
Canada Elections Act
engaged in sabotaging the efforts of those who believe in fighting for freedom. This should be looked into.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I do not think I am an Anglo-Saxon crackpot, either. Some of my people were natives of this country. It was the Conservative party that gave these people, senior citizens of Canada, the full franchise. This is the type of action we want. We want to broaden the franchise, not to restrict it. I am not at all sure that I believe the five year period of waiting before a person can become a full fledged Canadian citizen is reasonable, particularly if he has already been raised in the western tradition of freedom. I am not only speaking of the people from England, Scotland and Ireland but of people who have lived in the Caribbean all their lives, people with dark, yellow or black skins. The colour of the skin makes no difference, our Bill of Rights gives them all freedom here in Canada.
I should like to see the number of years of waiting before citizenship is granted reduced down to three years, or even to one year for those who are qualified. Our present immigration laws are restrictive. Canada has no right to deny millions of starving people the right to live. Why do we not open up our gates? Why do we not practice what we preach and broaden our immigration laws to encourage those who are willing to work and willing to defend freedom to come here and become a full-fledged citizen as soon as they are ready to expend their energy lives and resources alongside of us? I would like to see those who have fought in defence of the western world granted the right to Canadian citizenship. I would not hesitate to give anybody full citizenship in Canada who served Her Majesty in any corner of the world, particularly in time of war. Imagine denying a man who had been in the merchant marine in Australia the right to come to Canada and vote, or a man who had made seven or eight trips to England from Canada, carrying servicemen and ammunition in time of war.
I am against any restriction of the right to vote of people who, as I said, are qualified to be good Canadians. We should take a good look at the idea of restricting, for example, a well educated man, a professor from India or a doctor whom we would trust to operate on our children and be in charge of their health. Can we say to such a man: Oh no, you will first put in five years in Canada and will improve yourself in accordance with our view of western civilization. I do not think there

November 15, 1968
Canada Elections Act
will be many Russian spies voting, because we allow them to obtain full voting rights once they come here and start paying taxes. We deny a doctor making $20,000 or $30,000 a year and paying enormous taxes the right to vote, because he has not put in an arbitrary five year period in this country.
I fully agree with the hon. member who introduced this bill that we should take a good look at the voting rights of our armed forces, to make sure they receive the right to a secret ballot. They are the ones who paid the most and who intend to pay the most in their proper time for our freedom, for our right to have a country and our right to survive in this jungle in which we are living.
Let us not get carried away by the crocodile tears of people who say we should make immigrants wait before we grant them citizenship, or until we are ready to give those people who have already earned the right to full citizenship in Canada the kind of treatment they should get. Today the running down of anything Anglo-Saxon seems to be a kind of national pastime around here.
I say this is a red herring. It is not a question of whether or not you are Anglo-Saxon. The purpose of our reciprocal agreements with many nations of the commonwealth is to encourage commonwealth people to come here, and this is done for a very good reason. The very fact that these people are members of the commonwealth ensures that they are good risks and will adjust quickly to our Canadian way of life. Let us not have any more witch hunts here, and let us not seek cheap popularity by running down the Old Country because she does not happen to have the power she once had. I wonder how much more courage it would have taken to bring forward a bill such as this one a hundred years ago. It would not have been acceptable then and I do not think it is acceptable today, because it is restrictive and is in the nature of a witch hunt.
I would say most of the people who have come here from other countries are so glad to get here that they are not agitating for a vote, they are not here to tell us in Canada how to manage our position in the commonwealth. Most of them are so happy to be here that they have gone to work and are productive citizens who have taken their full place in the commonwealth. I should like to give them the full right to vote as soon as they show us they are no threat to this country, and thereby give them the right to say something about what is going to happen to the enormous taxes they are paying. The Americans broke

away from England because they said that people who were taxed had the right to have some say about it. If you feel so deeply about these people who are being so unfairly treated and who have no say about the elected members of parliament, and so forth, let me ask why they are not exempted from taxation until they become Canadian citizens. We bring them over here to use their skills. There is a brain drain in reverse going on in this country.
We bring these people here because we do not want to educate our own professionals. Let us give more of our own Canadian boys and girls a chance to become dentists and doctors, and not take advantage of commonwealth countries which need every doctor, school teacher and university professor in their own country. We have opened up a new university for these people who come here and when they see the good life in Canada they may be tempted to break the contract under which they came. We train these people so they can be a blessing to our sister commonwealth countries.
I venture to say that some of the people who write these letters want something more than simply to become citizens of Canada immediately. They want to tell us the rules under which they should be Canadians. I say we should beat them to it, we should certainly give them an easier franchise and an easier entrance to full Canadian citizenship, if they qualify.
It would be ridiculous to say to a man who served in the armed forces of Australia alongside of us for six or seven years during the last war, who speaks either French or English, either of our official languages, who is used to our parliamentary system and is thoroughly conversant with all our mores and has paid a tremendous personal price in service and sacrifice, that we have a witch hunt going on right now. It would be ridiculous for us to say to him: You are British and you have proved yourself British so we are going to make you wait five years, meantime we will take away from you a privilege which we gave to those people who qualify, for perfectly good reasons.
It is not because we love Englishmen or because we have put a racial tag on someone. This sounds to me like racism and I have the right to talk about it. Some of my people were natives of this country, who have been here for two or three hundred years. So I know what we have to offer in this country and I know it is not negative. We are not
November 15, 1968

denying others the right to Canadian citizenship which we have offered to people who have shown their loyalty to the crown, the commonwealth and our western principles and who have done so most often in very definite ways. We appreciate this, and we have given them an incentive to come here and give us some of their time and talents. I am getting a little bit tired of people who are trying to get on the bandwagon and who are picking on the poor old motherland because she is down. I see an element of that here, and it is not a very nice road to popularity.
Let us take the positive approach and offer full rights to those who come from our sister commonwealth nations. Let us not take the approach that if they do not play it our way we will not play it their way. We are the senior member of the commonwealth, we are the oldest child of the family. We should set an example, instead of being restrictive in dealing with voting rights in Canada. I do not know why we have a year of waiting, to tell you the truth.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I would be shocked if I went to any Commonwealth country and was told I had to wait for some time before I could vote. I have not done the homework the hon. member has done in relation to those countries which impose restriction on us, but I would be shocked if I went to Australia and, with my record, was told I could not vote for some time. I do not care how long we would have to live in Australia before we could vote; I think that is irrelevant. I do not believe that people from other parts of the world, perhaps from countries that have openly fought us or are going to fight us, should necessarily get equal treatment with people from countries that have proven to be friends and allies in the preservation of western democracy. Voting rights should be broadened by all means, but I do not believe I will stand in this house and vote for any restrictive measures on the rights of people from commonwealth countries who want to become Canadian citizens.
So far as citizenship itself is concerned, I venture to say a good many members of this house have not taken out citizenship papers. I agree that they should, but I am not sure that this is the proper way of forcing them to do so. Many of us were born here and have a certain distaste for the fact that we have to apply to obtain Canadian citizenship, especially in the light of the fact our ancestors have lived here for a hundred years. This
Canada Elections Act
little bit of red tape is annoying to some people, but it should not be so annoying that they do not apply for citizenship.
Citizenship is something we have taken for granted.

speechtext: I feel the hon. member has misunderstood the law and perhaps the hon. member for Calgary North could consult with him. The hon. member for Calgary North has suggested that citizenship does not depend on applying for a card. All of us have citizenship if we qualify under the law without applying for any papers. All I have suggested is that people who do not have citizenship should apply for it, not for a card.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING QUALIFICATION OF VOTERS AND CANDIDATES
speechtext:
Well, I think it is the thin edge of the wedge. I would go along with the hon. member if he suggested that all Canadians should seek Canadian citizenship if they desire it. However, I would not force it on anybody. Those who do not want to partake in the advantages of Canadian citizenship would please me if they never applied. I am certainly not anxious to have them vote if they are coming here from the commonwealth with no intention of becoming good citizens. I do not believe this is the case. I believe nine out of ten come here with the intention of earning a living and becoming fully qualified citizens.
I certainly do not believe the hon. member did so intentionally, but the letters he read contained overtones of racism. I certainly cannot go along with that. I see no necessity for bringing in the Palestine question, the coloured question or any other question. It is only a question of whether or not we are all Canadians and want to encourage as many people as possible to take part in public life and exercise their franchise. I felt this was the proper time to raise these other points

November 15, 1968
Canada Elections Act
about reform for our armed services personnel. Those who are in hospital should have every opportunity to vote. I know that in the five elections in which I have taken part I have been asked whenever I went to a hospital if the patients could exercise their franchise. We say we cannot do that because it is too difficult. Perhaps these patients are policemen who were hurt on duty, or members of the armed forces who are in hospital. We have put polls in some of the chronic hospitals and I feel this is a good reform. I think anyone who has the franchise in Canada should be given the right to use that franchise, even if we have to go to the trouble of hiring a few officials. Goodness knows, we spend money in many other ways which are not as important.
My Canadian citizenship is the source of my greatest pride. I do not like raising controversial issues like this. I think there is danger in this idea of telling our so-called new Canadians that they are being discriminated against, because I do not think they are. Perhaps we should say we have overlooked encouraging them, we have overlooked our duty to see that they become citizens. Perhaps we have been delinquent in not reducing this time limit. Certainly I should like to see any new Canadian who qualifies permitted to vote on an equal basis with those from the commonwealth. However, I would not take this backwards step of restricting the voting privileges of newly arrived Australians, New Zealanders, Caribbean people or Africans, regardless of their colour or creed. There are some Anglo-Saxon connotations to this idea. I honestly think it is a backward step, but I go along with the spirit in which I feel this suggestion was put forward. Let us broaden our franchise just as far as we possibly can without endangering security in Canada, by encouraging all those who want to be fully qualified citizens to take out their papers and be accepted into our family, with celerity.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING QUALIFICATION OF VOTERS AND CANDIDATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first to congratulate the hon. member for presenting Bill No. C-8, whereby, in order to take part in an election, to have one's name included in the list of electors or to run for office, one must be a Canadian citizen. This is I think a step towards the liberation in Canada from a certain type of colonialism that seemingly still persists in this country.
As it is now, the fact of being a British subject is sufficient for a person to be qualified

to vote, or to run for office, which would not normally permit people from New Zealand, from Australia, from Jamaica or other countries in the British Commonwealth to come to Canada and be candidates in a general election.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, that constitutes, I believe, a lack of respect for or a violation of our Canadian sovereignty. Canada is a sovereign country; we are told that it is and we say it.
To insist that anyone who wants to vote or run as a candidate in an election be a Canadian citizen does not mean that we reject completely everything that is British, of course not. Such a measure would not prevent us, for instance, from remaining a member of the British commonwealth of nations. India and other countries are members of the British commonwealth of nations, yet they enjoy their sovereignty.
Mr. Speaker, that would enable us, however, to be ourselves in Canada, to take our decisions ourselves, to be first of all Canadians. I am not saying that one should be an English Canadian or a French Canadian, but I say that one should be a first class Canadian citizen to have the right to vote or to run as a candidate in an election.
A couple of years ago, I presented a bill to the same effect but covering a much greater scope. It meant to remove from all Canadian acts references to British citizenship, keeping only the Canadian citizenship, without, as I said, Canada withdrawing from the British commonwealth of nations.
Mr. Speaker, I think the Canadian citizenship constitutes the fundamental quality of a Canadian and we would betray Canada and its identity by maintaining such references to colonialism. We have been a colony, French at one time, English at another, but we are no longer a colony. I believe Canada is an adult and sovereign nation.
And in that capacity, I believe Canada should assert herself more, while staying among the nations which make up the British community.
I shall now refer to the explanatory notes of Bill C-8, and I quote:
The purpose of this Bill is to provide that only Canadian citizens shall in future be qualified as electors or as candidates at elections:
November 15, 1968

The bill tends to amend paragraph (a), subsection (1), of Section 14 of the Canada Elections Act which would now read:
(a) is of the full age of twenty-one years or will attain such age on or before polling day at such election:
I am wondering, Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member who has prepared this bill should not have by the same token, taken into account the young people of 18 years and over. In the province of Quebec, these young people have the right to vote in provincial elections, while they do not have such a right in the federal elections. Here, I refer to an act which provides that in an armed conflict, for example, all young people of 18 years or over shall be called upon to serve their country.
When the government so decides, these same young people who must serve their country in the armed forces cannot have their say in electing their representatives as they are not eligible to vote or run as candidates at election time.
The time has come, Mr. Speaker, for our 18-year olds to be granted a little more consideration. If they are old enough to join the Canadian forces, they should be entitled to vote and they should have the privilege to run as candidates in any federal constituency. It is the law in Quebec. I do not know what the situation is in the other provinces, but the eligible voting age is 18 in the province of Quebec.
Furthermore, the hon. member introducing Bill No. C-8 should have included therein a useful clause dealing with compulsory identification cards for Canadian voters as a prerequisite to their names being printed on the voters lists, in addition to being Canadian citizens. An identification card bearing a photograph-I would not object to have my picture appearing on an identification card- would be a deterrent against those manipulating elections with the help of impostors or "phoney" voters.
Compulsory identification cards bearing photographs would avoid the stealing of elections. Perhaps we would have valuable members in this house who have been defeated because of trickery and shady election manoeuvring, mostly in cities where people are not known. In some instances, Mr. Speaker, women of ill repute disguised themselves as nuns in order to record their votes in well organized and controlled polls. This is contrary to true democracy. The people are no longer deciding when election schemers can arrange a choice.
Canada Elections Act
I think it is high time serious thought was given to a review of our election system, not only on the surface but in depth. As Canadians, let us still require that only Canadian citizens may have their names entered on the voters' lists and have the right to run as candidates.
In addition, let us lower the voting age to 18 and also make compulsory the identification card bearing the photograph of voter, for positive identification. Then we would no longer have to deplore the infortunate things that happened in the past and are still happening in many areas during general or partial elections.
This would eliminate a great deal of annoyances and also make things difficult for those who are inclined to use dishonest electioneering practices. In short, this would ensure the election to parliament of honest members through honest methods, both during and between election periods.
Mr. Speaker, those are the only remarks I wanted to make on Bill No. C-8.
I congratulate once again the hon. member for having introduced that bill providing that we should be Canadian citizens to have our names appear on an election list or to be a candidate at an election.
I regret however that an individual must have completed his twenty-first year instead of his eighteenth in order to vote or become a candidate.
The carrying of an identification card with a picture should be made compulsory to prevent the possibility of dishonesty, cheating or election gerrymandering. Thus, the Canada Elections Act would be more respectful of the Canadian citizens; the latter would more readily go to the polls to select their members and their government in order to establish in our country a true democracy based on social justice and the just society.

Mr. Speaker, I spoke just a few weeks ago in the private members hour on another bill to amend the Canada Elections Act. It seems to me that if a man's automobile needs minor repairs, it should be repaired or patched up. But if its poor condition has resulted from many points of weakness, then it either needs a thorough overhaul or else a new car altogether is required. In the same way, Mr. Speaker, if there are many points of weakness within the Canada Elections Act it

November 15, 1968
Canada Elections Act
seems to me we need either a thorough overhaul of the act or to write what might be called a new act altogether.
I am opposed to a piece by piece, or a bit by bit, or a patch-up approach to the revision of this act, and in that sence I am against this bill. As for the content of what Bill No. C-8 intends, I favour it in principle. It means, simply, Canada for Canadians; a Canada for Canadians, governed by Canadians; and I as well as other hon. members, I assume, support that. Yet there is an inequity within this bill, and I want to speak about that. Subsection (l)(a) says that only those who are 21 years old shall be allowed to vote.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
As you are well aware, Mr. Speaker, we live in a day when our citizens who are in their senior teens have been exposed to mass media literally from birth. This is a time when progressive forms of education are encouraging even very young children to develop their ability to discriminate, to judge, to decide and, hopefully, to learn to live with the results of their decisions.
This is also an era of high mobility for youth. Even at a very early age our young people spend many hours far away from their families and their environs; frequently they are many miles away. In such circumstances personal decisions are made at a very early age; they are made at a much earlier age than was the case, I suggest, even one decade ago. To have our voting age remain at 21 years of age is no longer consistent with the social context in which we now live. It ought to be lowered at least to 18 years of age and had this bill contained that change I could have supported it.
As for the idea that Canadian citizens and only Canadian citizens should vote to bring in a government of Canada, with that I have no quarrel. It is necessary for us to become more Canadian. I suppose it follows logically that we ought to be less British, less French, less Portuguese and less what have you, and we should be just plain Canadians. With that aspect of the bill I am in accord.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING QUALIFICATION OF VOTERS AND CANDIDATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I seem to have developed the habit of speaking on the Canada Elections Act. Only two weeks ago I spoke when another private member's bill to provide the franchise to university students came before the house. At that time I commended the mover of the resolution and said he was moving in the right direction. He is reform minded and

undoubtedly is aware of the inequities in the Canada Elections Act. My only reservation at that time was that the hon. member was not going far enough, although he was heading in the right direction. I suggested that the entire act needed revision.
I favour anything that tends to broaden the franchise and to make more democratic our Canadian parliamentary system. I am not in favour of anything that tends to discriminate. I was not in favour of those parts of the act which tended to discriminate against university students. I cannot see much use in tinkering with a document which, in my opinion, is of nineteenth century vintage.
If the Canada Elections Act were brought before this house and debated by all hon. members, I am sure we would arrive at a law which would constitute a new elections act. That needs to be done. I have read about the French revolution and I am aware of the great turmoil which surrounded the voting privileges of the common people of France. It took a revolution to undo the inequities surrounding the Estates General of France of that period.
I do not propose that we have a national revolution in Canada, but I do say that it is time for the government to take a good look at the elections act and to iron out some of the inequities in that act.
I could spend half an hour talking about the voting age alone, but I will not do so. As the hon. member preceding me said, we live in an age of great social change. Young people are being taxed, sometimes when they are only 16 years old. As my colleague indicated, taxation without representation was responsible for our great revolution in North America, as those who have heard about the Boston tea party will recall. In England they have considered this matter of the voting age, and there is every indication that in that regard they are more reform minded than we are. Perhaps hon. members ought to review what has happened in the United Kingdom House of Commons in this regard.
Some hon. members have said that under our system workers who are employed away from their electoral districts on voting day must return to their districts to vote. Sometimes they must travel a considerable distance to do so and no provision in the act makes it necessary for them to be paid a return fare to their jobs. People at sea especially are effected by this part of the act. During the last general election some people
November 15, 1968

in my riding were at sea on election day and therefore they could not vote. Many complained because of this. The returning officer in my district phoned to Ottawa, to St. John's to here and to there, but still those people went without their vote. Many of them were good supporters of both parties, yet they had no chance to vote.
